output:
I am asking for help maintaining the family photo importer that my aunt Mara and I use for the Keller family archive. It runs on a small computer in her dining room and copies pictures from phones, memory cards, and two older laptops into one dated folder tree. Joel, my cousin, checks the folders with her, but he does not change the importer itself. On Friday—no, sorry, on Saturday—we are planning to review the next import before Mara scans the envelopes from her parents' house. I want the instructions to reflect how we actually work and not assume that every picture has a date or a readable filename.

Mara usually brings home one card with about 400 images from a family gathering, and Joel connects it after dinner. The importer creates a folder for the year, then a folder for the month, and keeps each original filename when that name is usable. Last month, we had 37 files called image001 because two phones and one camera had reused the same names. The importer added a short device suffix to those copies, but we need to check that the suffix stays attached when the files are moved from the incoming folder into the dated folders. I do not know whether the older laptop exports will include the same camera information as the phones.

Please ask the maintainer to check the duplicate handling without deleting or renaming any original files. The importer should still make a separate review list when two pictures have the same date and nearly identical sizes, because they might be copies, but Mara sometimes takes a still photo and a burst frame a few seconds apart. She wants those left for a person to compare, not automatically merged. Joel said, “Last time the review list was clear until the card reader disconnected, and then we could not tell which batch it described.” Could the batch name include the card label and the import date so they can identify it later?

There is also a small setting that matters when we restore the archive after a computer problem. Mara asked me to keep this key enabled and to confirm that it keeps the original image bytes unchanged when a rotated preview is made. The preview can be adjusted for viewing, but it must not replace the file copied from the card. If the key is missing from the configuration, please ask before adding a default, because we are not sure how the older backup computer was set up.
archive.retain_originals

On the living room computer, the import directory has folders from 2016 through 2024, and the shared drive has a second copy up to 2022. The 2023 and 2024 folders are only on Mara's computer for now. She asked that the next run copy new files to the shared drive, but not move or remove anything from the existing directories. If the shared drive is unavailable when the import starts, then the program should wait and show a plain warning rather than silently writing a second incomplete archive on the computer.

Section one: The checks we would like to discuss. Point one: Confirm that a card can be scanned in a read-only way before copying. Point two: Show the card label, the import date, and the number of files found before Mara confirms the run. Point three: Keep a record of skipped files with the reason each was skipped and the path where it came from. Point four: Let Joel export that record as a text file for the family notebook. These are requests for review, not a demand to change the way old folders are named. The notebook uses short descriptions like “lake weekend” and “Aunt Nora birthday,” and it is useful to keep those labels even when the camera date is blank.

Mara told me, “If a picture has no date, please do not guess from the folder it landed in. I would rather mark it unknown and ask Joel.” She does sometimes know the event from a handwritten note on the envelope, but that note may cover a whole roll rather than an individual frame. If she types a date for a roll, the importer should ask whether the date applies to every undated picture on that roll or only to the selected one. We have not decided which choice is safest, so I want the maintainer to describe the current behavior before proposing a change.

For a practical check, we can use a spare card with 12 sample pictures: three with the same filename from different devices, two without date metadata, and one pair that look alike but have different file sizes. Mara can supply that card, but she has not checked whether its small video clip should be included in the test. Joel can compare the copied originals against the card using the computer in the dining room. Please do not treat a preview rotation as a change to the original, and do not count the preview files as additional imported photographs. The sample card also has a text note named “scan notes” that should remain beside the card copy.

We would like the maintainer to tell us which reports already exist and whether the import date in those reports uses the computer clock or the date recorded by the camera. That distinction matters because the computer clock was set incorrectly for 11 days in October last year. The family corrected the folder labels by hand, but nobody wrote down which files were affected. I am not asking for a reconstruction of that period. I only want to know whether a new batch report would make the chosen date source visible and whether an uncertain camera date can be marked without changing the image metadata.

Finally, please keep the discussion focused on this importer and the next family archive run. Mara is available on Tuesday evening, and Joel can join after seven, but neither of them can test a new version before the weekend. If the maintainer needs a sample folder, we can provide a copy of the 2021 picnic folder with names and dates as they currently appear. Last spring, our board-game lending shelf moved from the narrow hall beside the music room to the wide alcove near the east entrance. The change happened on April ninth, after the building manager finished replacing a loose floor tile and painted a yellow line around the new shelf area. The lending group had eleven regular volunteers and about eighty games at the time, and we wanted visitors to find the games without walking through a class in progress. I am describing the move because the forwarding of one note became important to how we handled the first month of the new arrangement.

Before the move, Elian Cruz kept the paper sign-out sheet in a green folder and tracked overdue games on a small calendar. He said, “People ask where the shelf is even when they can see it from the desk.” The new alcove faced the reception counter, but a tall plant partly blocked the view from the main door. We moved the plant to the window on the following Monday and left a strip of blue tape on the floor to show where visitors could stand while reading the rules. The tape was not meant to mark a queue, and the sign said that in plain language near the bottom.

Our shelf rules allowed each household to borrow two games for fourteen days. A household could request one extra week if nobody else had reserved either game. Returned pieces had to be counted at the table rather than in the hallway because dice and tokens had previously rolled under the radiator. The shelf was open whenever the building was open, except during the Thursday after-school club, when the alcove served as a quiet room. Volunteers still took returns at the desk then and placed them in the red tray until the club ended.

1. The blue binder holds the sign-out sheets and the list of volunteer shifts.
2. The red tray is only for returned games that need a piece check.
3. The yellow card beside the shelf has the reservation instructions and the library phone number.
4. The small black box contains spare pencils and blank return slips.

Elian made this list for the new volunteers after two visitors put completed slips inside the binder and one volunteer stored a returned game in the pencil box. The list stayed inside the cabinet door rather than on the public notice board because it included the phone number for the volunteer lead.

On April seventeenth, a family brought back Foxes at Dusk with one wooden marker missing. They had borrowed it on opening day and returned it in the red tray with a note saying that the marker might be inside the cloth bag. The game was not reserved, so the volunteer on duty could wait until the next shift to check every piece. If it had been reserved for that afternoon, she would have called the family before lending it again. That condition mattered because the reservation card only showed the game title and the first name of the next borrower.

The volunteer checked the box under the game insert and found the marker caught in a folded corner. The family had also left a small paper map they had drawn to show where they found the loose pieces. The map was not part of the game and was returned to them on their next visit. Elian wrote the repair date on the inside inventory card and left the reservation card unchanged. The same afternoon, two people asked whether the game could be held past closing, and the volunteer explained that a reservation did not extend the building hours.

On April twentieth, I was asked to forward the shelf group's note about the new location to the neighborhood bulletin editor. I used the address from the contact sheet and forwarded the note before the evening shift began. The note said the shelf had moved to the east alcove and listed the hours and borrowing limit. It also asked readers to bring games back with all their pieces and to use the red tray for returns that needed checking. Elian said, “Please keep the last line about the Thursday club because it saves a trip for families.” I kept that line in the note.

The editor replied the next morning and said the bulletin would run on Friday, but that the map needed a shorter label. She asked whether “east entrance alcove” was the approved location wording, and I checked with the building manager before answering. He confirmed that the public directory called the place the east alcove and that the entrance phrase could make people look for a separate room. I replied with the directory wording, and the editor sent back a proof that afternoon. The group had no request to change the lending rules, so the proof only changed the location label and the order of the contact details.

At the end of April, we counted seventy-six games on the shelf and four in the red tray. Two needed replacement pieces, and one had a reservation waiting for Saturday. The volunteer lead taped a fresh copy of the hours beside the yellow card because the old copy had curled near the radiator. The plant stayed beside the window, and the blue floor strip stayed in place. We kept the green folder at the reception desk and continued using the paper sheets while the group discussed whether to make a digital list. Nobody had approved a change to the sign-out process.

The first month in the alcove went smoothly, but the group still had small jobs to finish. Elian planned to bring a ruler to check that the yellow card was level, and the volunteer lead wanted to ask the after-school staff whether the quiet room schedule would change in summer. We left both tasks on the next meeting agenda rather than guessing at an answer. Families continued to ask about the extra week, and volunteers pointed to the reservation rule on the card. The forward note remained in the bulletin file, and the editor's proof was clipped behind it for anyone who needed to confirm the published location.

preview.show_labels

Archive Preview Setup: The North Quay Collection

The North Quay archive is preparing a preview of records from the former harbor office, a two-room building that stood beside the ferry landing from 1912 until 1978. The preview is meant to help researchers understand how the collection is arranged before they request boxes in person. It includes selected descriptions, a small set of scanned documents, and practical information about visiting the reading room. The project team is using a temporary site that mirrors the archive’s catalog structure without exposing internal staff notes or restricted records.

Mara Venn, the project archivist, began by comparing the catalog export with the inventory completed during last winter’s move. She marked eleven folders whose titles had changed when the records were rehoused, then checked each new title against the folder labels and transfer sheet. One entry described a bundle of ferry schedules as “unidentified timetables,” although a note inside the folder named the vessel routes and years. Mara retained the catalog title but added a concise scope note explaining the dates and routes. “A visitor should be able to tell what a folder contains without mistaking our description for the original label,” she said during the planning meeting.

The preview uses three levels of description: collection, series, and folder. The collection page gives the dates, extent, creator, and a short account of the harbor office’s work. Series pages group records by function, including passenger services, maintenance, and correspondence. Folder entries provide titles and dates, with selected notes where the original wording is unclear. The team kept the same hierarchy used in the catalog so that a researcher can move from a broad subject to a particular folder without learning a new filing system. They also decided not to display every folder in the collection, because several groups have not yet been checked against the current inventory.

A numbered review plan guides the next stage:
1. Compare the preview list with the signed inventory and note any unmatched identifiers.
2. Check names, dates, and place references against the folders, not just the older catalog export.
3. Confirm that each selected scan has a matching description and a stable file name.
4. Review the access note for every item chosen for display, including documents with personal information.
5. Test the pages on a phone and a laptop, then record any navigation or legibility problems for correction.

The digitization assistant, Ilya Chen, prepared scans of a 1936 tide table, two maintenance notices, and a marked-up map of the east pier. The originals vary in size and condition: the tide table is a narrow sheet with a fold through the printed columns, while the map is a large drawing with pencil annotations at the edges. Ilya saved preservation masters in the archive’s imaging workspace and made smaller access copies for the preview. The descriptive records link to the access copies, not the masters. File names include the collection code, folder identifier, and a sequence number, which lets staff distinguish the two maintenance notices without relying on their nearly identical titles.

The preview’s display options were tested with sample records before the full selection was loaded.
preview.show_labels
That setting places the catalog’s field labels beside values such as “Creator” and “Dates.” The labels remain useful on a narrow screen, where a visitor may otherwise have to infer what a short value means. Mara asked for a second check of long descriptions because the first sample made the scope note appear as one dense block on a phone. The web editor now keeps paragraph breaks in the displayed text, while the internal export retains the original line endings for staff review.

Access checks depend on the documentation attached to each item. The harbor office’s public notices and routine schedules are available for the preview, but a small group of employment files remains closed under the archive’s access policy. If a permission record does not include a review date, staff leave the related item out of the preview until they can verify its status. That condition matters for the photograph folder: its inventory entry lists three employee portraits, but the accompanying permission sheet has no date. The folder therefore stays off the public selection list while the archivist checks the accession paperwork. The preview may include other photographs from the same series when their records are complete.

Nora Bell, who maintains the reading-room information, drafted the practical details for visitors. The archive is open Tuesday through Friday, with appointment requests handled by email at least two working days ahead. Researchers should bring a photo identification document and may use pencils or personal laptops at the tables. The building entrance is on Wharf Lane, not the ferry road shown on some older maps. Nora included the nearest bus stop and explained that the public entrance has a small step and a portable ramp. She asked the team to distinguish the reading-room schedule from the staff office hours so that the preview would not imply that records can be consulted without an appointment.

During the first review, cataloger Dev Patel found that the east pier map had been assigned to the maintenance series even though the inventory places it with engineering plans. He checked the folder, the transfer sheet, and a handwritten register from the harbor office. The register described the map as a working plan used during a railing repair, which explains why it had appeared with maintenance material in an earlier arrangement. The current inventory reflects the archive’s decision to group technical drawings together. Dev updated the preview record to match that arrangement and added a note about the map’s repair annotations. He left the old catalog reference in the staff-only crosswalk so that earlier citations can still be traced.

The team also reviewed how search results behave when visitors enter different forms of a place name. The harbor office used “North Quay,” “North Wharf,” and, on a few forms, “the ferry quay” for the same location. The preview retains the wording found in each original title and uses a controlled subject entry to connect the variants. A search for any of the three terms can therefore lead to the relevant records, although the displayed title does not silently replace the language on the document. Dev tested searches for “tide,” “pier,” and “passenger,” then checked that each result opened the correct description rather than another record with a similar date.

Before loading the remaining scans, Ilya recorded image dimensions, file sizes, and the page order for each selected item. The map requires a larger access copy than the notices because its edge annotations are part of the evidence and would disappear at a smaller scale. The tide table needs no color adjustment; its faint blue ruling is visible in the current scan, and the printed figures remain legible at ordinary screen size. Ilya entered a brief technical note for the map and tide table so staff can reproduce the access files if they need to. The technical notes are not part of the public description, but their identifiers match the files linked from the preview.

Mara’s closing review covers both what visitors can see and what staff will need to revisit. She checks that each displayed item has a title, a date or a clear statement that the date is unknown, and a link that opens the intended scan. The team records unresolved questions beside the relevant inventory identifiers rather than in the public text. At the next review, they will return to the photograph folder if the permission record gains a review date, compare any corrected descriptions with the physical labels, and check that the preview still follows the current inventory. The remaining selected records will be added only after their descriptions, access notes, and file links have been checked against the same working list.

So this is about the shared folder sync client at the Harbor Arts office, and I'm dictating the handoff for Mara and Devin because they cover the front desk on different days, and the folder has to keep working when neither of them is in the room. The folder is called Winter Inventory, and it sits inside the office team space, not in my personal drive. The client runs on the Windows laptop by the packing table and on Mara's MacBook, and there is a small tablet that only shows the files; it does not upload anything.

We started changing the setup on Monday the fourth, after the label printer stopped seeing the current stock sheet. The client showed a blue cloud beside the folder name and said it was up to date, but the file on Devin's laptop was still the Friday copy. We checked the account first rather than deleting anything because the local archive had two years of invoices, and nobody knew whether those were already in the team space. Devin said, “If we reset this before we know where the invoices are, I'll have to call the accountant.” So we left the archive where it was and made a separate folder called Old Invoice Check inside the office team space.

Mara asked me to make sync.limit_uploads stop allowing background uploads on the tablet. The request is for that setting to limit uploads there, not to pause downloads and not to change the desktop behavior. The tablet is on the guest Wi-Fi, and it sometimes tries to send the whole photo roll when Mara only opens a stock photo. We kept that distinction in the setup note because the stock sheet still needs to arrive on the tablet even when uploads are limited. The exact key from the note is on its own line here:
sync.limit_uploads Use fresh fictional people, details and wording for this independent episode.
I read the key aloud as sync dot limit underscore uploads and copied it from the settings panel rather than typing a different spelling.

Then I checked the network and saw that the packing table laptop was using the office Ethernet connection, while Mara's MacBook was on staff Wi-Fi. The router had restarted at 6:20 in the morning, and the client had queued three changes at that point. None of the three was a conflict. The changes were a new supplier address in the contact sheet, a revised count for brass hooks, and a scan of the delivery slip. We let the laptop finish those uploads before changing the tablet because otherwise the order of the updates would have been hard to explain.

There are two ordinary limits on the office account. The shared folder has a storage allowance of 18 gigabytes, and the current contents use 11.6 gigabytes. The client can hold 30 days of deleted files in its recovery area. The 18 gigabytes is the folder allowance, not the laptop disk size, and the 30 days is the recovery window, not a promise that an offline device will keep every older version. I repeated those roles in the handoff because last month someone read the recovery window as a sync delay and waited a day for a missing scan.

For the setup checks:
1. Confirm that Winter Inventory is selected and not the archive.
2. Confirm that the account shown is the Harbor Arts team account.
3. Open preferences and find the uploads section.
4. On the tablet only, turn the limit on for background uploads.
5. Leave downloads enabled.
6. Wait for the blue cloud icon to return before closing the client.

The desktop menu uses slightly different wording, but the same folder name is visible. We did not change the desktop upload setting, and we did not ask anyone to remove old files. The check on the tablet took about seven minutes, and the laptop stayed connected throughout.

At 10:15, Mara opened the stock sheet on the tablet and saw the new supplier address, but she did not see the delivery slip yet. The slip was a large scan and was still downloading, so we waited instead of refreshing the folder. Devin said, “The address is there, so the connection is back, but let's give the scan another minute.” The scan appeared at 10:19, and Mara confirmed that it opened without a warning. We did not treat that as proof that every file on every device was current, only that this sheet and this scan had arrived.

One issue remains with the tablet. When it is on guest Wi-Fi, the client may show a gray cloud while it is waiting for a connection, and that icon does not tell us whether the upload limit is on or off. The preferences page is the place to check the limit. If the tablet is taken to the storeroom and the gray cloud stays there, then bring it back to staff Wi-Fi before changing any settings. If the icon turns blue after that, leave the client open for a few minutes and check the sheet again. If it stays gray, write down the time and the network name and tell Mara; do not reset the client, because the local photo queue has not been reviewed.

Before leaving, I put a paper copy of the steps in the top drawer beside the barcode labels and sent the same notes to Mara and Devin. The copy says the tablet setting applies only to background uploads, the download setting remains on, and the desktop setting remains as it was. It also says that the archive folder is for checking the old invoices and is not a replacement for Winter Inventory. No one has confirmed that the old invoices are duplicated in the team space, so that check is still open on the list for Thursday. The next person on the front desk can use the working stock sheet in the meantime, but if a new invoice scan arrives, keep it in the team space and tell Devin before moving anything else.

For the Thursday setup at the north desk, Mara Velez asked me to configure the desktop uploader for the Alder Street archive room. The machine is a Windows workstation called Juniper, and it shares a wired connection with the scanner. The uploader will send scanned intake packets to the city records server, not to the public website. Mara said she wants the folder named incoming intake on the desktop to remain the place where staff review files before sending them. She has four clerks who use that computer, and they do not all sign in at the same time. The uploader should start when a clerk signs in, but it should not open four copies if someone clicks its shortcut twice. The scanner makes PDFs at 300 dpi, and the usual packet has between 8 and 24 pages. Mara asked that the original scans stay unchanged, even if a clerk later adds a note to a separate review copy.

The server address is records alder archive dot local, and the destination folder is /drop/intake/2025. The year in that folder is part of the server path and should not be changed when the calendar year changes, because the records manager keeps the annual folders together under that name. The desk is scheduled to send packets from 7:30 in the morning until 6 in the evening on weekdays only. The server may be offline during the Tuesday maintenance window from 12:15 to 12:45. The uploader should wait and try again after that window rather than show a failure for every file. The network team gave Mara a maximum of 3 retry attempts for a failed connection, with a delay of 90 seconds between attempts. Those numbers refer to connection retries, not the number of pages or the time allowed for a clerk to review a packet. Mara said, “If it is still offline after the third attempt, leave the packet in the queue and tell the clerk what happened.”

The draft configuration currently has the resume option turned off, and Mara wants it enabled because some intake packets are large and the connection has dropped twice during the first week of testing. Use this exact key on its own line:
transfer.allow_resume
Set its value to true. She also wants completed uploads removed from the local sending queue only after the server confirms receipt. If the connection drops before that confirmation, the local item must remain available for another attempt. Do not delete the original scan from incoming intake after a successful send. The records server returns a receipt number, and the uploader should save that number with the sending time in a log beside the application files. There is space for 14 days of logs on the workstation, and the records manager copies those logs to the archive each Friday.

Mara asked me to check the alert choices with her rather than assume that every warning should be emailed. The four clerks share one team mailbox called intake desk at alder archive dot local, and none of them has an individual uploader account. The machine can also show a desktop notice while a clerk is signed in. She wants an immediate notice for a rejected file and a notice if the queue still has an item waiting after 20 minutes. She does not want a notice for each ordinary successful upload, because a busy morning can include 30 packets. The daily summary should list the number of files sent and any files still waiting, but it should not include scan contents, names of clients, or copies of the PDFs. Send that summary to the shared mailbox at 6:10 in the evening on weekdays, and skip it on Saturday and Sunday. The 20 minutes is the waiting threshold for a desktop notice, not a deadline for deleting or rejecting a packet.

Setup checklist:
1. Install the current uploader build 5.4.2 from the approved software folder and confirm that it opens under each clerk account.
2. Choose Juniper as the workstation label and select the city records server profile. Then check that the destination reads /drop/intake/2025.
3. Set the weekday sending window to 7:30 in the morning through 6 in the evening, and enter the Tuesday maintenance period from 12:15 to 12:45 as a pause.
4. Enable the 3 connection retries at 90-second intervals. Then do one test with a two-page sample PDF and confirm that the receipt number appears in the log. The two-page sample is only for the test and does not change the normal packet size. The clerks said they would rather test with a copy than with a real client packet.

There are two file types that the server rejects: a PDF with a password and a file larger than 40 megabytes. The normal 8 to 24 page packet is usually under that limit, but some packets include color photographs. Mara asked for a warning that names the rejected file and gives the reason without attaching the file or changing its name. If a packet is over the size limit, the clerk should be able to make a smaller review copy and try that copy separately, but the original must remain in incoming intake. The same rule applies to a password-protected file: after a clerk makes an unprotected review copy, the uploader should not remove or alter the source file. The team mailbox is for notices only and should not be set as a location for scanned documents.

When I asked what to do if the workstation is shut down during the sending window, Mara said, “Let the queue wait until the next time a clerk signs in. Do not start the computer remotely.” The uploader should resume queued work after sign-in if the server is available, and should keep the weekday schedule rather than sending overnight. There is no request to install the uploader on the scanner or on the records manager’s laptop. Juniper is the only workstation in this setup. The records manager wants to check the first week’s log on Friday afternoon and compare receipt numbers with the server list before anyone changes the retention period. If the logs fill before the Friday copy, the uploader should show a warning and keep its queue intact. No one has asked for automatic deletion of old logs.

Final note for the handoff: Mara asked me to leave a short setup note beside the workstation with the server profile name, the destination path, the retry settings, and the name of the shared mailbox. She wants the note to say that the 20-minute alert is only a prompt to check a waiting item, not proof that an upload failed, and that an item stays queued until receipt confirmation. She also asked me to tell the clerks that the 6:10 summary counts files rather than pages, and that Saturday and Sunday have no scheduled sending window. If the network team later changes the maintenance period, the Tuesday pause can be updated without changing the weekday sending hours. For now, leave the schedule and all stated values as they are, and make the test using only the two-page sample.

This is the dye room log for Thursday, the twelfth of June, dictated by Mara Voss at the North Quay Textile Workshop. The morning shift opened the east mixing bay at six forty and checked the two kettle gauges before anyone moved the wool lots. Kettle one held at thirty-eight degrees, and kettle two read thirty-seven and a half. The wall thermometer was three degrees lower, so I asked Dev to check it against the brass hand gauge. He did and wrote that the wall unit was slow, not the kettle dials. The lot on the first trolley was wool flannel from batch W eighteen forty-six, in twelve rolls, with a total dry weight of ninety-six kilos.

The requested shade was Harbor Slate from the April card, but the card had faded on its lower edge, and the small square looked greener under the east window. Mara compared it with the retained sample from the May run and called for the blue-violet concentrate rather than the plain navy. Dev said, “The retained square is closer to the coat lining than the card is,” and I said, “Right,” because that was the reason we kept a control square from May. The mix sheet called for six hundred grams of blue-violet concentrate and one hundred and eighty grams of charcoal concentrate per fifty kilos of dry wool. The scale was checked with the one-kilo brass weight before the first measure. It settled at one thousand grams exactly, and the empty stainless scoop was tared between colors.

First, the wool was wetted in clean water for twenty minutes. The water came from tank three and measured at pH 6.4. After soaking, the crew lifted the rolls one at a time and let each drain for two minutes before loading the kettle. Dev asked whether to add salt with the first concentrate or wait until the dye bath turned over. Mara said, “Add it after the wool is moving, because the folds on this flannel hold color unevenly if the salt goes in too soon.” She pointed to the pale stripe near the selvage on the previous trial roll. That stripe was recorded on Tuesday and was not treated as a stain; it followed a tight fold in the cloth.

The actual first rinse began at eight—no, nine fifteen—after the kettle had held at seventy-two degrees for twelve minutes. The earlier time was my false start from reading the rinse column instead of the dye column. We used the lower drain trough because the upper trough was still carrying the cream linen from the night shift. The valve was turned toward the blue mark, and Dev checked that the cream water had stopped before the wool came through. The rinse took eleven minutes. The outgoing water was still faintly blue at minute eight and clear enough at minute eleven. The crew saved a jar from the first drain and labeled it “Thursday first rinse” for comparison with the next slate run.

At the break, Nico brought over a small card with a note from his aunt, who had worked at a mill near Porto. She had written “tá, fica bom,” meaning “okay, it looks good,” beside a photograph of the blue-gray fabric. He told us tá is what she says when she agrees that a color is acceptable, not when she is hesitating. He was pleased that the new sample matched the photograph more closely than the April card. Dev read the card twice and said he would keep the Portuguese words on the sample sleeve because they explained why Nico had marked the photograph as an approval of the shade, not as a batch instruction. Nobody added the aunt's note to the formula sheet.

1. The first retained swatch is the dry control cut from the left end of roll four and marked with the date and batch number.
2. The second swatch is the wet control taken after the eleven-minute rinse and clipped to the back of the log sleeve.
3. The third swatch is from the right end of roll twelve and is being held for the afternoon light check. Do not sew the three together. The edges are different, and the comparison needs each swatch to remain separate. Dev wrote the same directions on the envelope and used pencil because the outer paper may be replaced.

At ten thirty, Lena from finishing came to check the fabric under the north skylight. She said the face looked slightly cooler there than beside the kettle, but the shade did not shift toward green. She asked if the whole lot should be dried before the shade was signed off. Mara said, “Not yet. Keep two rolls damp until the afternoon check, and dry the other ten on the low rack at forty-five degrees.” Lena noted that the damp rolls were numbers three and nine and tied them with white cord. The condition matters because if either damp roll shows a pale fold after drying, the crew must reopen the dye assessment before the lot is packed. If both match the control squares, they can remain in the regular finishing queue. No one has made that check yet.

On the lower shelf, the team found an older notebook with a line in German from the previous consultant: “Er hängt das Muster um neun ans Fenster.” Dev translated it as, “He hangs the sample by the window at nine,” and explained that um in this sentence means “at nine” rather than “around the window.” The old line referred to a separate cotton trial and was not copied into today's shade record. Mara asked him to keep the notebook open to that page until the archive clerk came because the handwriting on the facing page might identify who had changed the cotton temperature. The entry does not name a person, and Dev left the name field blank.

At noon, the bath log showed a final temperature of thirty-four degrees and a pH reading of 6.7. The used liquor was moved to the marked recovery tank rather than sent to the floor drain, as a sample jar was still being compared with the Tuesday trial. Nico weighed the leftover concentrate containers and recorded two hundred and sixteen grams of blue-violet and sixty-eight grams of charcoal. He returned both lids tightly closed and put the containers on the locked shelf. The scale was wiped dry and checked again with the brass weight before the afternoon team used it. One of the trolley wheels had left a short blue mark near the drain. Lena wiped the floor and added the cleaning time to the room board.

Mara closed this part of the log at twelve twenty. She left the two damp rolls on the low rack with the white cords visible and placed the three separate swatches in a paper sleeve marked “Harbor Slate comparison.” She wrote that the retained May square was the closer color reference than the faded April card and that the blue rinse jar should remain beside the sleeve until the next slate batch is assessed. The afternoon light check is still pending, and the finishing decision for rolls three and nine depends on what the crew sees after drying. The other ten rolls are recorded as drying at forty-five degrees. The archive notebook remains open for the clerk, and the dye room will continue with the cream linen only after the lower drain trough has been rinsed and checked.

The request concerns slip C14 at North Quay, which is beside the old stone steps and across from the fuel shed. The boat is a 26-foot sloop with a blue hull, a cream stripe, and a small wooden name board near the stern. Its registration number is MA7429Q, and the owner is Mara Voss, who lives on Cedar Lane in Bellhaven. She asked me to send the full request with the dates and access details rather than only asking whether there might be room.

Mara said the boat has been kept at C14 since early April and that she has paid the monthly mooring charge by bank transfer on the fifth of each month. She said, “I am asking for the same slip through next season if the harbor schedule allows it.” She does not say that the renewal has already been approved, and she has not received a confirmation from the office. The dates she requested are April 1 through October 31 next year. She can bring the boat back during the last week of March if the harbor staff need to inspect the cleat and the dock line before the season begins. She would like any reply sent to her email address, and she will also check the mailbox at the harbor office when she comes by on Friday afternoons.

There are a few details about the location that may help the staff review the request. The slip is on the inside of the North Quay and faces the public walkway. The nearest water connection is fixed to the post beside C12, while the electrical outlet is on the shore-side post at C16. Mara said she uses the water connection only to rinse the deck and does not leave a hose stretched across the walkway. She keeps one shore power cable aboard and stores it in a gray locker under the forward berth. The mooring line at the bow is 12 feet long, and the stern line is 10 feet long. She asked that the office note the existing arrangement because the cleat at C14 is lower than the cleat at C13, and a longer bow line rubs against the edge of the dock in a strong east wind.

It asks staff to include any available alternative dates if those dates do not work and to say whether an updated insurance page or another boat photograph is needed. The boat remains at C14 until the current arrangement ends on October 31, and Mara will wait for the office reply before making a plan for next season. We are maintaining the family photo importer that brings pictures from phones and memory cards into the shared archive, and this is my update for the next work session. The importer is used by my sister Leah, my uncle Peter, and me, and none of us is comfortable losing the original files. So the request is to make the next version easier to check without changing the way the family names its albums. The old laptop is still running the current copy, and the replacement laptop has a test library with photographs from our own trips.

The importer should read the date taken field when it exists and use the date the file was copied only when the camera date is missing. Last Saturday, Peter tried twelve pictures from a small camera, and four had no date taken value. The other eight went into the April Coast Walk album with their camera dates. The four without dates went into an album called Undated Review rather than being mixed into the current month. Please keep that distinction visible in the log, and do not treat an empty date as proof that a picture was taken today.

The most important setting is archive.retain_originals and it must remain enabled while the importer makes smaller display copies for the family website. The original camera files should stay untouched in the incoming folder until a person checks the import. The setting is used on the test laptop as well as the old laptop, and the family wants the same value on both machines. The scan should report if the setting is absent, but nobody has asked for the importer to delete or repair a setting automatically. The original filename should also remain visible beside any shorter display name so Leah can compare the two.

Duplicates are another concern because Peter sometimes copies a card twice before he has sorted the first batch. The importer currently flags files with the same size and matching image contents, but it should not decide that two photographs are duplicates only because they were taken on the same day in the same place. A burst of six pictures of the pier can look almost alike and still show different waves. The family wants a review row for a likely duplicate with both filenames and both dates shown side by side. Do not remove either file during that review. The person doing the import will choose what to keep.

1. Confirm that an import of twenty-seven files reports twenty-seven scanned files, even if three are placed in Undated Review. The scanned count is the number of files read from the card, and the review count is a separate number.
2. Use a card with two copies of the same beach image and one similar but different image. The exact copy should be flagged for review, and the similar image should remain a separate entry.
3. Check the display copy by opening it on a phone and make sure it is small enough to load on the family website while the original remains full size in the incoming folder.
4. Unplug the card after the scan has finished and confirm the log still shows the source card name and the album chosen by the person doing the import.

These are checks for the test session, not claims that the current build already passes them.

On the old laptop, the family folder has seven named albums, and the test library has two extra albums that are only for test photographs. This happened on Friday, April 12, at the North Quay station in Bellhaven when I went to exchange tickets for a weekend trip to Alderwick with my aunt Lena. I had bought the tickets online through the Coast and Valley Rail site three weeks earlier and printed the confirmation at the library because our home printer was out of ink. The original journey was Saturday morning and the return was Sunday evening. We were staying with my cousin near Alderwick Market and planned to carry one small suitcase each, plus a folded walking frame for Lena. The frame had a label with her name and phone number, but no medical details on it.

I had the booking email on my phone and a paper copy of the confirmation with reference QV 48291. The original outward train left Bellhaven at 9:18 and arrived at Alderwick at 11:06, with a change at Fenmere. The return train left Alderwick at 5:42 on Sunday and reached Bellhaven at 7:31. I had picked the aisle seat because Lena prefers to sit near the window, and I had chosen seats across the aisle from each other. When I read the names aloud at the counter, I said the return passenger was my aunt Lena, and the clerk checked the spelling against her photo card. The ticket had Lena as Leena, but the rest of the name and the date of birth matched.

The clerk was called Nadiya, and she explained that the outward train had a replacement coach on one part of the route, so the connection at Fenmere was only nine minutes. She said the exchange desk could move us to the 8:36 train with a twenty-minute connection, or leave us on the 9:18 service if we preferred. I asked whether the earlier train would still reach Alderwick before lunch, and she said it was scheduled to arrive at 10:51. She also explained that the printed ticket was an advance fare, so any change had to be made before the original train departed, and the fare difference would be charged per passenger.

I told her I wanted to exchange both tickets but not change the return journey because we had already arranged for my cousin to collect us after the Sunday train. I asked if there was a charge for correcting the spelling on Lena's ticket and whether the walking frame counted as a second piece of luggage. Nadiya said the spelling could be fixed while she reissued the ticket and that the frame was allowed as a mobility aid. She did not say that the exchange had been completed then; she first needed to check seat availability on both trains and confirm the difference in fare. I kept the old tickets on the counter so I could compare the times before agreeing.

There were three details I asked her to check: first, whether two seats across the aisle were available on the 8:36 service; second, whether the new tickets would still show the Fenmere connection clearly; and third, whether the exchange receipt would list the extra fare separately. The seats we had on the 9:18 train were coach B, seats 14 and 15, and Lena had asked not to be placed beside the door because the movement of people makes it harder for her to stand safely. I said we could sit in another coach if the seats were together across the aisle and not in the first row. Nadiya wrote those preferences on a yellow slip and told me they were requests rather than guarantees.

While she checked the fare, I called my cousin Arlo and told him the possible arrival time might change. He said he could meet us at the station either way, but asked me to send the final train details by text because the station entrance on Market Street was being repaired and the usual pickup bay was blocked. I asked whether he could bring the wider car rather than his small hatchback so the walking frame would fit without being folded again. He said the wider car was available after 10:30 and that he would wait by the temporary taxi rank if we arrived on the earlier train.

Nadiya then said the exchange could go ahead if the 8:36 train still had two suitable seats and if the fare difference was no more than eighteen pounds in total. I said that was right and asked her to pause before charging the card if either condition was not met. She checked the screen and turned it slightly so I could see the seat map. There was one aisle seat and one window seat across from it in coach D, and they were not in the first row. She said the total difference shown was sixteen pounds and forty pence. I asked whether the connection at Fenmere remained nine minutes, and she said yes, but the arrival board showed the connecting platform was usually beside the incoming platform.

Before I handed over my card, I asked Nadiya to read the itinerary back because I had once confused the return date on another booking. She read: Saturday, April 13, from Bellhaven at 8:36, changing at Fenmere and arriving at Alderwick at 10:51; then Sunday, April 14, from Alderwick at 5:42, arriving at Bellhaven at 7:31. I checked that both passenger names appeared on the outward and return coupons and that Lena's spelling had been corrected. She said the updated confirmation would be sent to the email address already on the booking and that the printed exchange receipt would show the amount paid at the counter. I gave her the card only after she confirmed the two conditions were satisfied.

After the payment, I asked for the old tickets back because the confirmation number on the paper copy was still useful if the email took a while to arrive. Nadiya returned them with a small stamp across the front and handed me the new itinerary and the receipt. She reminded me to keep the receipt until the journey was over and said the platform information could change on the day. I put the new papers in the blue folder with Lena's photo card and the walking frame label, then read the arrival time aloud to her. She said 10:51 would give us time to find the station lift before Arlo arrived. I texted him the times and the temporary taxi rank location while we were still inside the station lobby.

When we left the exchange desk, the old confirmation was still in the folder and the new paper showed coach D with seats 14 and 16 across the aisle. I checked the date once more and saw that the return remained Sunday, April 14, rather than Saturday. I also wrote down the exchange receipt number 61038 in my travel notebook in case the paper copy was misplaced. Lena wanted to know whether there was a cafe near the Fenmere platform, and I said I would look at the station map before Saturday. We walked out by the side entrance because the main doors were crowded, and I kept the folder in my coat pocket until we reached the bus stop.

This is the delivery account for the Saturday market stall at Alder Quay, and I want to get the order of the morning down while it’s still clear. Mira Solis runs the stall called Little Orchard, and she was expecting one delivery from North Field Cooperative before the first customers arrived. The truck was due at seven fifteen, and the stall opens at eight. The delivery mattered because the orchard association had arranged a tasting table beside her stand, and their volunteers were bringing visitors over in groups. Mira had asked for crates of pears, apples, and late plums, plus two boxes of paper tasting cups. The forecast said there could be a light shower, but the market was still going ahead.

On Friday, Mira sent the driver a message that the unloading point was the east gate beside the blue fish mural. The west gate is blocked by the repair crew this week, so the driver was meant to use the east gate and call her when he reached the ramp. She also said the small service lift was working, but only if the driver kept the door button pressed until the crates were inside. Otherwise, it timed out and needed resetting. This condition came up later because the driver was alone for the first part of the delivery and had to bring the hand truck through the lift one load at a time.

At six forty, the stall team arrived in a borrowed van and found that the alley behind the market was wet but not slippery. The tablecloths and chalkboard were in the van, along with a folding canopy and a roll of spare price labels. Jonah Reed, who helps Mira on Saturdays, put the canopy legs beside the stall and checked each locking pin. He said, “I can keep the rain off the tasting cups, but the side flap needs to stay open so people can see the fruit.” Mira asked him to leave the chalkboard blank until she had confirmed the prices, because North Field sometimes changes the price for late plums if the harvest boxes are smaller than expected.

At seven twenty, the truck still had not appeared, and Mira called the cooperative office. The dispatcher said the truck had left the depot at six fifty, but the driver had reported a slow queue on Harbor Road. Mira said, “Please tell him not to circle round the west side. The road works have closed that entrance.” The dispatcher repeated the east gate instructions and said she would send a text when the driver was close. While they waited, Jonah placed the cups on the lower shelf and kept them inside a covered tote because the shower had started. He did not put out the fruit signs yet because the prices were not confirmed.

At seven thirty-eight, the driver, Elian Park, called from the east gate. He had reached the blue mural, but a delivery cart was parked across the ramp, and he could not bring the hand truck through. Mira went down with Jonah and asked the neighboring flower seller to move the cart. The seller was arranging buckets and said, “Give me two minutes and I will clear a path.” She moved it within a minute, and the truck was unloaded at the curb. Elian had six pear crates, four apple crates, and three plum crates, plus two boxes of tasting cups. The packing slip listed the plums as twelve kilograms, but the scale at the cooperative had weighed them at eleven point six kilograms. Mira took a photo of the slip and wrote the scale reading in her notebook rather than changing the printed number.

First, Elian carried the paper cups and two pear crates to the stall. Then he brought in the remaining fruit in trips, using the lift. He remembered to hold the door button down as he moved each load. The lift did not time out, and nobody had to reset it. The apples were packed in shallow trays with cardboard between the layers. The pear crates were deeper and had loose straw around the fruit. One apple tray had a split corner, but none of the apples had fallen out. Mira checked the tray against the slip and marked it as received with a note about the packaging. She left the other trays closed until Jonah had cleared enough room on the display table.

Numbered section for the checks that were made at handover:
1. The pears were counted as six crates, and the labels showed two varieties: Bartlett and Bosc.
2. The apples were counted as four trays, and the split corner was photographed before the tray went onto the lower shelf.
3. The plums were counted as three crates, and the measured weight was recorded as eleven point six kilograms against the twelve kilograms on the slip.
4. Both boxes of tasting cups were present, and the outer box on top had a damp patch, but the cups inside were dry.
5. Mira kept one copy of the signed slip in her cash tin and gave the driver the other copy. She did not ask for a price adjustment at the stall because the cooperative office handles weight differences on Monday.

After the fruit was inside, the shower stopped, and Jonah opened the side flap of the canopy while Mira wrote the prices on the chalkboard. The orchard association volunteers arrived at seven fifty and asked whether the tasting could begin before the market opened. Mira said they could set out a small sample of pears, but they should wait on the plums until the stall team checked that the fruit was cool and firm. She cut one pear and one apple and put the pieces on a clean plate. The pear was ripe but still held its shape, and the apple was crisp. The plums stayed in their crates because the top layer felt warmer than the apples.

By eight ten, the first visitors were at the tasting table, and the volunteers directed them from the quay path to Little Orchard. Mira told Jonah to keep the damp cup box under the counter and use cups from the dry box first. If the damp patch spread inside the box, they were to stop using that box and tell her before opening it. The patch did not spread during the morning, and the inner wrapping stayed dry. Elian left after Mira signed the slip and took a picture of the clear east gate ramp as proof that the cart had been moved. The market stayed busy until noon, and the remaining plums were kept for sale without changing their price. The delivery was complete before opening, and the only note still waiting for Monday was the weight difference on the plum slip.

I am forwarding the winter access notice to the shed committee before the first week of November because the south gate schedule is still unclear and the members need the same information before they choose their lockup hours. The notice came from the property office on Tuesday and names the shared bicycle shed at Alder Court. It says the courtyard lights will be tested after sunset on November sixth and that the gate may remain open for up to twenty minutes while the electrician checks the sensor. The office has not given us a confirmed start time, so I am forwarding the notice as it arrived, not as a final schedule.

The shed has twenty-four numbered floor loops and a narrow aisle between the repair bench and the north wall. The blue rack near the entrance belongs to no one in particular, but residents use it for pumps and spare lights. Mira Solis keeps a paper map in the weatherproof box because the painted numbers on loops seventeen and eighteen have faded. She told me, “The map saves arguments when somebody comes home late.” The committee has asked that the map stay in the box and that nobody tape a new sign over the emergency contact card. The card lists the building caretaker and the after-hours maintenance number.

Last Saturday I counted six bicycles in the aisle and one folded trailer beside the bench. The trailer was dry, but its fabric cover had slipped onto the floor and blocked the lower drawer where we keep tire levers and patches. I moved the cover onto the bench and left the trailer where it was because the owner was not there. The repair bench has a small lamp with a cracked shade and a labeled jar for valve caps. People sometimes leave wet gloves on the radiator pipe by the west wall, though the pipe is not a drying rail and the caretaker has mentioned that it gets warm during the evening cycle.

Ravi Patel has been measuring the doorway because he wants to know whether his cargo bicycle can turn without touching the shelving. He measured the narrowest point at eighty-six centimeters and wrote the figure on a yellow card beside the map. His bicycle has a long rear deck and a child seat that he removes before bringing it inside. He said, “I can wait until the delivery boxes are gone, but I cannot lift the back end around that corner.” The delivery boxes belong to the seed library and are usually collected on Thursday mornings. One box was still there on Friday when the caretaker made the weekly walk-through.

The rain gauge on the courtyard fence is easy to miss because a climbing plant has grown across its lower half. Jules Kim cleared the leaves from the opening but did not move the gauge or cut the plant back. The maintenance note says the paving contractor will inspect the drain only if the gauge records more than twelve millimeters of rain by Friday at noon. If the reading stays below that amount, the inspection will be put off until the next visit. Jules asked that nobody empty the gauge before the caretaker records it and wrote the request in the small notebook beside the entrance. The notebook also has entries about a loose hinge and a missing reflector.

The notice includes a small checklist for the evening of November sixth. The list is spoken as five entries:
1. Check that the aisle is clear from the entrance to the bench.
2. Leave the emergency contact card visible in the weatherproof box.
3. Keep the blue rack available for shared pumps and lights.
4. Write down the rain gauge reading before anyone empties it.
5. Tell the caretaker if the gate stays open longer than twenty minutes.
The checklist does not ask residents to move another person's bicycle, and it does not give anyone permission to change the gate timer. The electrician is expected to test the sensor with the caretaker present, but the notice does not say who will arrive first.

Mira said she can meet the electrician if her shift ends before six, but she has not confirmed that she will be there. Her work timetable changes from week to week, and she asked me to leave her name off any fixed appointment list. Ravi can be at the shed after seven on Wednesday and Thursday, but not on Friday because he takes his daughter to swimming lessons. Jules is away through November fifth and plans to check the rain gauge when she returns that afternoon. These are possible times to reach people and not promises that anyone will attend. The committee has not chosen a person to wait at the entrance.

The property office asked residents to send questions by email rather than leave notes under the caretaker's door. The email should include Alder Court in the subject line and the words “bicycle shed” so staff can sort it from repair requests about the courtyard apartments. One resident asked whether the electrician will need access to the locked storage cupboard. The notice does not answer that question, and the cupboard contains folded chairs and a box of donated helmets. Another resident asked whether the gate will be held by hand during the test. The property office said it would ask the electrician but has not sent a reply yet. The committee is collecting the questions in one message.

There are small practical details that should remain visible in the shared record. The entrance mat curls upward at its east corner after heavy rain. The spare key is kept in the caretaker's office and is not stored in the weatherproof box. The yellow card with Ravi's doorway measurement should stay beside the map rather than on the repair bench, and the blue rack has a loose foot that rocks when someone leans on it. The caretaker said the rack should be reported instead of tightened by residents because its base is fixed to the floor by two bolts. The next committee meeting is planned for November ninth in the laundry room, and the agenda includes the gate test, the drain inspection, and the faded loop numbers.

If the rain gauge reaches more than twelve millimeters by Friday at noon, Jules wants the committee to include that reading in its message to the property office and ask whether the paving contractor is still expected to inspect the drain. If the reading is lower, she wants the message to say only that the threshold was not reached and that the note can be revisited at the next visit. The caretaker asked me to forward the winter access notice now so residents can check their own schedules and send questions before the test. I am forwarding it with the measurement, the checklist, and the unanswered cupboard question included, and I will keep the original arrival time marked as unconfirmed.

output:
I am forwarding the notebook scans from the north fork traverse to Mara Ellis because she is assembling the autumn basin record and asked for the pages before the survey team leaves on Friday. The notebook belongs to the Ridge Station collection, and the blue cloth cover is split beside the lower brass hinge. I carried it in a padded map case from the old pumphouse to the field shelter on Tuesday afternoon and set it on the dry shelf above the sample trays. The pages smell faintly of wet cedar, but none of the pencil marks ran in the rain.

The first entry is dated September fourteenth and begins at the basalt ledge above Willow Creek. We reached the ledge at six forty in the morning after taking the east switchback rather than the washed out creek path. The barometer read eight hundred and twelve millibars, and the wind came steadily from the northwest at about twelve kilometers per hour. Evelyn Park used the hand lens to check the pale crystals in the dark matrix while I measured the exposed face with a folding rule. The rock was roughly three meters high and seven meters across, with a narrow seam that continued behind a patch of lichen. Evelyn said, “That seam is too straight to ignore, but we should not call it a fault until we see the contact at both ends.” I copied her words beside the sketch and marked the uncertain boundary with a dotted line.

At ten fifteen, we followed the ridge toward the western saddle and found a band of loose shale beneath the fir roots. The upper layer was gray brown and broke into thin plates, while the lower layer held small iron colored grains and a few rounded quartz pieces. There were no fresh tool marks, and the fern cover was flattened only along the narrow animal track. We noted the location with the station compass and wrote the bearing as two hundred and thirty degrees from the cairn. The notebook also records a second reading from the base of the slope because the compass needle wavered near the metal buckle on the pack. The two readings differ by six degrees, and neither one has been crossed out on the page. Jonah Bell suggested checking the bearing again at the next marker, and I wrote that request in the margin rather than choosing a preferred reading.

Section Four: Numbered Notes
1. The wet patch below the shale band measured about four paces long and one pace wide.
2. Water was visible at the surface, but no stream channel continued through the grass.
3. The ground felt firm under the heel at the upper edge and soft near the willow roots.
4. We left the small stones where they were because moving them would have disturbed the thin moss layer.
5. Evelyn photographed the exposed grains with the scale card beside them and logged the image time as eleven oh six.
6. I entered the sample location in the notebook only as a reference point and did not collect a specimen there because the site boundary on the old map is difficult to read.
7. Mara asked us to keep the original map notation even where it disagrees with the newer trail sheet.

After lunch, we checked the lower ravine from the footbridge and compared the color of the water with the earlier notes. The water was clear in the center and clouded close to the bank, where fine silt had gathered around the roots. No one crossed the barrier tape because the bank edge had slumped since the spring visit. From the bridge deck, I could see two parallel bands in the cut face and one thin orange streak just above the gravel. Evelyn estimated that the orange streak was less than two centimeters thick and said, “It may be surface staining, but the page should show exactly where we saw it.” I drew a small arrow from the label to the streak and added the word possible before the description so the notebook would not read as a confirmed mineral identification.

The return route took us past the north marker, where a wooden post had tilted toward the trail. The brass tag was still attached, and its number matched the station register, but the small white paint mark below it was nearly covered by mud. Jonah brushed only the loose mud away with a glove and left the paint untouched. We recorded the post angle as approximate because the ground around its base was soft and there was no level surface for the clinometer. I also wrote down that the trail crew had placed a new orange ribbon on the spruce to the east of the post. The ribbon was not on our map, and we did not move it or treat it as a boundary marker. On the last page of the day, Evelyn listed three items still to check: the western contact, the compass reading at the saddle, and the source of the iron colored grains. Mara's request was to leave those entries open until someone could make a second visit.

The condition for the later catalog is that if snow covers the north marker before the second visit, then the team should use the bridge reading as the starting reference and note that the post itself could not be checked. That condition is written beneath the date in the same graphite as the route notes. It is not a prediction about the weather, and it does not replace the six degree difference in the compass readings. I have put the loose leaf sketch behind the page with the wet patch measurements because its pencil arrow points to the same willow roots. The sketch has no separate date, so I wrote the notebook page number in its upper corner without adding a location that we did not record.

The final entry says that the field shelter was locked at five twenty and that the sample trays remained in place on the dry shelf. The notebook went into its cloth wrap before we left, and the map case stayed with me overnight. Mara asked for scans of the route pages, the numbered notes, and the final open items; she did not ask for the cover photographs or the station register. I am forwarding those notebook scans to her now with the original page order intact and with the two uncertain readings visible. No scan includes the loose register or any page from the winter survey. The final line of the notebook is a reminder to bring a fresh scale card on the next traverse, and the line ends with a small pencil mark after the word traverse.

I am forwarding the April community survey export to the Neighborhood Records Group because the library team needs one shared copy before the open house on May 17. The export covers six blocks around Cedar Square and includes responses collected from March 4 through April 29. It has 186 completed forms and 12 partial forms, and the partial forms remain in a separate tab. The file name is cedar_square_survey_april_final, and the tab names are Overview, Responses, Access Notes, and Follow Up. The word “final” is part of the file name, but the group has not marked the export as approved. This is the version prepared by Mara Ellis after she checked the response count against the paper intake log.

At the top of Overview, the survey asks residents how they use the square during an ordinary week. The choices are walking through, attending events, sitting outdoors, and using the play area. People could select more than one choice, and there was also a write-in box. The largest number of selections was for walking through, followed by sitting outdoors. The export does not calculate a single total of residents for those answers because one form can include several selections. Mara said the percentages are based on completed forms and should not be read as a count of unique visitors. That note is already in the first row of the Overview tab.

The Responses tab has the original answer text beside a short category assigned for sorting. The category is not meant to replace what the resident wrote. For example, one response says, “The path is easy in the morning, but the benches fill up after school,” and its category is “seating and timing.” Another resident wrote, “I can hear the music from my apartment, but I cannot get across the square with my walker,” and the category is “route access.” Mara kept both comments in the export because the first mentions a time of day and the second describes a barrier that may not appear in a checkbox answer. No names or apartment numbers are included in that tab.

The Access Notes tab has four records that need a closer look before anyone uses the figures in a public handout. Two residents left the question about mobility blank, one response lists both the west gate and the fountain as an entry point, and one paper form has a date written as April 31. The date is outside the calendar, but the paper log shows that it arrived with the April 30 batch. Mara has not changed that record. We are handling the ceramics delivery for the north room at the Bellweather Community Arts Building, and I am forwarding the revised delivery sheet to Mara Voss at the front desk before the truck leaves the depot. The order comes from the Alder Creek Pottery Cooperative and includes forty-eight dinner plates, twenty-four shallow bowls, twelve serving platters, and six blue-glazed water pitchers. The pottery packed the pieces in nine cartons and one narrow crate. The crate holds the pitchers upright and has a red paper label on both short sides. The plates and bowls are in cartons marked with a white moon; the platters are in cartons marked with a green square. The driver is Lewis Grant, and his truck number is thirty-seven. The delivery window on the sheet is from nine thirty to ten fifteen on Thursday, May 4.

The road into the Arts Building has a low stone arch, and the truck cannot pass beneath it. The driver needs to stop at the gravel lay-by beside the old pump house, then roll the cartons through the west service entrance on hand carts. Mara told me the entrance door sticks if the outside temperature is below eight degrees, and she has put a rubber wedge in the blue supply cabinet for that reason. The route from the lay-by crosses a tiled courtyard with a shallow drain near the fountain. There is a temporary board over the drain, but the board shifts when a cart wheel catches its edge. The building caretaker says the board will be secured before the delivery arrives. The caretaker also asked us to keep the loading area clear for a piano tuner who is expected at eleven.

The pottery asked for a signature at delivery and a count of every carton before the driver leaves. Mara will sign the delivery sheet, but she will not sign the damage form unless she has checked the pieces herself. She has arranged for Dev Patel from the studio to be there with a clipboard and a small flashlight. Dev will inspect the outer packing and record dents or wet patches without opening a carton. The pottery said that any broken glaze or chipped rim should be photographed beside the carton label and reported to its office by the end of the day. Mara said, “If anything arrives damp, leave the paper around it until I can look at the carton.” No one should use the tall shelves beside the kiln because the lower brackets are loose, and the shelves are being repaired next week.

The room is prepared for the delivery, but the tables are not all in the same place. The folding table near the sink is reserved for the pitchers, and the long maple table is for the platters. The plates should stay on their original cartons until the class teacher comes in the afternoon. She wants to check the glaze colors against two sample tiles. The sample tiles are in a padded envelope inside the locked drawer of the red desk. The key is with Mara, and the drawer sometimes catches when it is pulled straight out. Dev knows to lift the handle slightly before opening it. There are four blue cotton pads in the red desk for the pitchers and two rolls of brown paper under the maple table. No one has ordered packing foam for this delivery.

Section Three: The count to use when the truck is at the entrance.
1. The first count is nine cartons and one narrow crate.
2. The second count is forty-eight plates, twenty-four bowls, twelve platters, and six pitchers.
3. The third check is that the red labels stay on the short sides of the crate and the white moon and green square remain readable on the cartons.

Mara wants the carton count written in the left margin of the delivery sheet. The piece count goes in the box marked “contents,” and the time the last item enters the building goes in the box marked “received at.” Dev should note whether the blue cabinet wedge was used and whether the courtyard board stayed in place. These are separate observations, and he should not combine them into one comment.

The forecast on the wall calendar shows light rain around noon, but the delivery is scheduled before that. The canopy above the west entrance is narrow, and water runs from its left corner after a long shower. Mara asked the caretaker to place a dry runner inside the door rather than across the courtyard. The runner has a dark rubber backing and a paper tag that says “west entrance only.” The spare runner in the closet is cream-colored and belongs to the gallery. If rain begins early, the driver can wait under the canopy while Dev checks the cartons. The pottery office number is printed at the bottom of the delivery sheet, and Mara has written the studio extension beside it. The office closes at four thirty and does not monitor messages on Sunday.

The driver called this morning to ask whether he should bring the empty hand carts back to the depot. Mara said the Arts Building has two carts of its own, and the driver may take his carts away after unloading. She also asked him to leave the narrow crate beside the folding table instead of putting it under the table because the crate has a fragile base. The delivery sheet lists a wooden brace inside the crate, but the brace is only for transport and should stay with the crate if the pottery collects it later. Lewis said, “I will keep the crate upright and leave the brace where it is until someone from the cooperative gives me a collection date.” Dev will put a small sign on the crate so the evening cleaning crew does not move it.

If the kiln room temperature is above twenty-four degrees when the pottery arrives, the cartons must remain sealed in the west room until the class teacher can move them to the cooler cabinet. If the temperature is twenty-four degrees or lower, the cartons may be opened after Dev has recorded the labels and Mara has signed the count. Dev will read the wall thermometer before anyone opens a carton and write the number beside the received time. This condition matters because the blue glaze can soften when it warms too quickly. Mara has not asked anyone to change the kiln setting, and the caretaker has not promised that the room will be cool. The thermometer was checked last Monday, and the caretaker plans to check it again on Thursday morning.

The Arts Building will keep the delivery sheet in the red desk after the driver leaves, and Dev will place any photographs in the shared ceramics folder before closing time. Mara wants the picture files to include the carton label and the damaged area in the same frame when possible. If a label cannot be seen without moving a carton, Dev should photograph the damage first and write down the label instead of lifting the carton. The class teacher expects to arrive at one thirty and needs the west room clear enough to set out her sample tiles. The cleaning crew comes after six and will not enter the west room if the small sign is still on the crate, so Mara will remove it after she has checked the delivery. The final count, the temperature reading, and the driver signature should all remain on the same sheet.
