Last Thursday, I was at the north room with Mara and Devin, looking at the shared-folder client on the archive laptop. The team calls the folder field-notes, and it sits under the studio share. Mara said the client had shown a green check beside the folder since breakfast, but she could not tell whether that meant every file had reached the other two computers or only that the laptop had finished its local scan. I asked her not to call it complete yet because the status panel had not refreshed since 8:12, and the laptop was still on the guest wireless network.

Devin was trying to keep the client available for the afternoon catalog work without letting it use all the upload capacity. He asked, “Can you set the client so it sends no more than 3 megabits per second while the call is running, and then let it use the normal connection after the call?” I said I could make that a temporary setting, but I wanted to check whether the limit applied to this computer or every device connected to the shared folder. He said the setting is on the laptop only and asked me to leave the other two computers unchanged. I opened preferences and read the key aloud as “sync dot limit underscore uploads.” No, wait, the label is written with a period after sync and an underscore between limit and uploads.

sync.limit_uploads Use fresh fictional people, details and wording for this independent episode.

Mara showed me the queue before I changed anything. It had 18 items waiting: 11 were image files from the camera import, and 7 were small text or spreadsheet files. The oldest queued item was a 640-megabyte scan named harbor-map-final.tif, and it had been waiting since 7:46. The client showed a yellow pause icon beside that scan, but no warning beside the other items. Mara said she had paused just that file yesterday because she was not sure whether its duplicate in the review folder had the same annotations. I said I would leave the file paused and not remove either copy until she could compare them.

I read the current upload rule from the settings screen. It was set to automatic, and there was a separate option to limit uploads on this device. I did not change the automatic download setting because Devin had asked about upload speed only. He said the video call was booked from 1:30 to 2:15, and the limit should apply only during that period. If the call moved or ran late, he wanted me to ask before extending the limit. I said, “If the call ends early, I will not turn the limit off until one of you confirms that the call has ended.” He answered, “Yes, that is right. Please do not guess from the calendar.”

1. Before the call starts, check that the laptop is connected to the studio wireless network and that the client has signed in as mara.ellis@example.net.
2. Apply the 3-megabits-per-second upload ceiling on this laptop only, and note the start time in the handover sheet.
3. Leave downloads at automatic and leave the paused scan alone.
4. Check the status again at 2:15, but if the call is still in progress at that time, keep the ceiling in place and ask Devin whether it has ended rather than turning it off on schedule.

I asked whether the team wanted the remaining 17 items to move in their current order or whether the spreadsheets should go first because the inventory meeting was on Friday. Mara said, “Keep the existing queue order for now. The oldest item should stay paused, and the other 17 can proceed as the connection allows.” She added that there was no need to make a copy of the queue list because she had already exported a record at 8:05 to the folder named client-logs. I did not open that export, and I did not verify its contents, so I wrote down only what I could see in the live queue.

When I opened the handover sheet, I found an older note saying the ceiling had been 2 megabits per second during a test in May. Devin said that was for a different call and should not be reused. I asked if the new ceiling was 3 megabits per second or 3 megabytes per second. He said, “Megabits, as written in the request, because the client displays the rate in megabits.” I repeated that back to him, and he said, “Correct. Also, the 18 in the queue is a count of files, not megabytes, and the 640 megabytes belongs only to harbor-map-final.tif.” I added those distinctions to my spoken note so nobody would confuse the file count with the transfer rate.

Mara wanted one more check before anyone left the room. The laptop battery showed 46 percent, and the power adapter was plugged into the strip under the desk. Devin asked me to put the condition about the call in plain language in the handover note, and I wrote that the upload ceiling stays on past 2:15 if the call is still running, and that I should ask him before changing it once the call has ended.

I left the remaining items in their displayed order and recorded that the next person should check the client status at 2:15, check whether the call has ended, and then follow Devin's answer rather than assuming the limit can be removed. Tuesday morning, I spoke with Elian Park at the Willow Bend Ceramics workshop about the delivery scheduled for the Old Ferry Building in North Harbor. The order has six cartons of serving bowls, two cartons of blue glazed pitchers, and one long crate of display tiles. I’m Mara Vell at the North Quay records room, and this is the setup note for the desktop uploader on my desk machine. I’m asking Ivo to configure ParcelDesk 4.8 before the catalog team starts sending the spring map scans on Monday. The computer is a Windows 11 workstation named atlas-07, and the account that should run the uploader is M Vell, not the shared intake account. The app is already installed and opens normally, but it still points to my old test folder. The new source folder is D:\quay\maps\ready, and the destination is the North Quay Archive collection called Coastal Sheets 2025. Please leave the separate invoices folder out of this job because those files belong to finance and are not part of the map batch.

We have 184 scanned sheets in the ready folder today, and the largest file is 212 megabytes. The scanner team expects another 30 sheets by Friday, so the queue should be able to hold at least 220 files without making a second collection. The maximum size for one file should be 250 megabytes, and the uploader should divide larger transfers into 16-megabyte chunks. The current files are TIFF scans plus a small group of PDF indexes. Do not convert either type before upload because the preservation team wants the source bit depth and the index text left as received. The machine has 16 gigabytes of memory, and the app can use 2 gigabytes while the batch is active without affecting the image station next to it.

Please use the archive gateway at gateway.northquay.example and keep the region set to East Bay. The collection owner is Elian Cho, and the project code is NQ Maps 25. Use that exact project code in the uploader description field. The contact address for notices is mapsdesk@northquay.example, not my personal address. The gateway credentials are already saved in Windows Credential Manager, so don’t put a password in the configuration file. If the uploader asks for a second sign-in, stop and ask me rather than trying the shared intake account. The server certificate name should read archive.northquay.example, and the app should use the certificate already installed by IT support.

1. Access and destination: First choose the M Vell Windows profile, then point the source at D:\quay\maps\ready. Select the Coastal Sheets 2025 collection and enter NQ Maps 25 in the description box. The uploader should preserve each original filename and add no prefix or date stamp. The archive team has asked us not to rename items because the scanner labels match the paper folders. If a filename already exists in the collection, compare the checksum and show me the conflict rather than replacing either copy. The map index PDF files should stay in the same collection as the TIFF sheets.

2. Transfer behavior: Set the queue limit to 220 files and allow 6 transfers at once. The network team said the wired connection is stable during the day, but our guest wireless can drop when the public meeting room is full. Use the office Ethernet connection whenever atlas-07 is docked, and if that connection disappears, keep the current transfer paused and wait for the wired connection to return. Do not switch to guest wireless or a phone hotspot. Set the retry limit to 4 attempts with a 30-second wait between attempts. If all 4 attempts fail, leave the item in the queue and show an alert rather than marking it complete. The settings should not start another attempt every few seconds because the gateway team monitors repeated connections.

transfer.allow_resume

3. Checks and local files: Calculate a SHA-256 checksum before sending and compare it with the receipt from the archive gateway. If the values do not match, keep the local original and the incomplete transfer record, and alert me. Do not mark that file as complete. The temporary chunk folder can be cleared only after the gateway receipt matches and the item appears in the collection. Keep the activity log for 14 days and include the filename, time, and outcome for each attempt. The log should not include credentials or the full contents of a scanned page. Use the default Windows event location for errors, and put normal batch activity in the ParcelDesk log folder under Local App Data.

4. Timing and notices: Start the first test with 3 files from the ready folder at 9:15 on Tuesday, and send the result notice to mapsdesk@northquay.example. If the test finishes without a checksum mismatch, then leave the rest of the batch queued for my review. Do not release all 184 files automatically at that point. The team will add the next 30 sheets by Friday, and I want to check the filenames and collection count before the larger transfer begins. Set the normal transfer window to weekdays between 8:00 in the morning and 5:30 in the afternoon, and leave weekend transfers disabled.

I spoke with Elian yesterday, and she said, “Please keep the original scan names because they are written on the folder tabs.” That is why the filename rule matters, even for the indexes. Ivo also said the gateway may be unavailable during the archive maintenance window on Thursday from 6:00 to 7:00 in the evening. If a queued transfer reaches that window, let it wait until the next permitted weekday window rather than extending the schedule. The uploader may stay open after 5:30 so the status is visible, but it should not send data outside the transfer window. If the machine restarts during a paused transfer, restore the queue when M Vell signs in and show which files were still waiting.

Before changing the settings, please send me a screenshot of the destination and transfer pages so I can verify the collection and retry values. I am not asking for the test to be run before Tuesday, and I don’t want a sample upload sent to another collection. Once the first 3 files have been checked, I will tell Ivo whether to release the remaining queue. The status panel should show total files waiting, completed files, and any checksum alerts in separate counts, and it should display the last successful gateway connection time. These details will help the map desk answer questions without opening each record. Keep the desktop shortcut where it is now, and do not change the scanner profile because that belongs to the imaging staff.

we had the intercom repair meeting in the laundry room at alder court on tuesday morning because the lobby panel had been cutting out and residents were missing deliveries. i was there with mara ellis from the building office, joel pike from northline access, and mrs chen from 4c, who keeps the paper log for the east entrance. the panel still lit up when we arrived, but the sound dropped whenever somebody pressed the silver call button. joel said the wiring cabinet was dry and the problem seemed to be near the speaker grille, not in the basement power supply. nobody said the unit was ready, and we did not set a date for closing the repair ticket.

mara had printed the service notes from the last two visits and put them beside the sign in sheet. one note said the sound had returned for about an hour after the door closer was adjusted in april. the other said a delivery driver had heard a buzz from the panel but no voice from 4c. mrs chen said she had been home both times and had answered through her kitchen handset. she told us the lobby unit was quieter than that handset, but it was not completely silent. joel asked us not to press the call button over and over because a loose contact could make the test confusing.

we talked first about forwarding the lobby calls to mara's office phone while joel checked the speaker and the cable behind the panel. mara said, “i can keep the office phone near me until four, but i have a lease appointment at half past two.” joel said the forwarding setting could be temporary and would not change the numbers stored for individual apartments. mrs chen asked whether the resident handsets would still ring as usual. joel said they should, and that the test was meant to cover only the lobby call button. he had not tried the temporary setting yet, so nobody treated that as a result.

the office phone sits on a shelf behind the mailboxes, and the signal there is usually steady unless the loading door is open. mara said that on tuesdays the parcel carrier often leaves the loading door propped for a few minutes, even though the sign asks drivers to close it. joel wanted to know whether the phone had to stay at the desk or could be carried to the entrance. mara said it could be carried, but the charging cord was short and the battery indicator had been blinking since monday. we agreed to keep the phone at the desk for the first part of the check and to note the time of each lobby call.

then we went through the work in order. number one inspect the grille for lint and paint, without taking the faceplate off. number two check the small connector behind the panel and make sure the cable was not pinched against the frame. number three use the office phone for forwarding during a single test call, while one person stood in the lobby and another stayed by the desk. number four write down whether the sound was clear at both ends, and whether the door closer or the loading door changed anything. number five return the setting to normal after the test, unless mara asked joel to leave it in place until she had checked with the building manager. joel said he would bring a narrow screwdriver, a flashlight, and two spare clips, but he did not expect to replace the panel.

mrs chen said she could listen from 4c if the test took place before her afternoon medication delivery. she was not asking for the call to be forwarded to her apartment; she wanted to hear whether her own handset sounded different from the lobby speaker. mara wrote that distinction in the margin so nobody would mistake it for a request to change her apartment settings. joel said we could ask her to pick up once, after the lobby test, if she was still home. the delivery usually came between one and two, but the driver had arrived close to noon the previous week, so we left the time flexible.

we also checked what residents had been told. a small notice by the mailboxes said the entrance intercom might be tested, but it did not name a time or say calls could reach the office. mara said she had not sent a building wide message because we did not yet know how long the check would take. mrs chen said some residents do not read the paper notices, especially the people who use the west entrance. joel suggested putting a second notice near that door, and mara said she could do that after the office phone was free. no one asked residents to leave their doors unlocked, and we did not plan to interrupt calls from apartment handsets.

there was one condition that could affect the afternoon plan. if the lobby door was still locked at six because the evening cleaner had not arrived, mara said she would not leave the office phone unattended by the entrance. she could keep it at the desk and ask the caretaker, devon, to stand by the panel for any later test. devon usually arrived at six fifteen, but mara had not confirmed his route for that day. joel said the temporary forwarding could be turned off before he left, and that we should not assume a missed call meant the speaker was fixed or broken. we wrote the condition beside the time notes rather than treating it as a confirmed arrangement.

before we left the laundry room, mara read back the notes aloud and asked whether anything important was missing. mrs chen said to include the faint clicking sound she heard after pressing the call button, and joel added that the click might come from the button itself rather than the speaker. i said the office phone battery and the loading door should both be mentioned, since either could affect what we heard during the test. mara said, “i will keep the phone on the desk, and i will tell you if i have to leave for my appointment.” the final line on the sheet said the next check would depend on joel's arrival time and the office schedule. the repair ticket was still open, and we had not recorded a result from the forwarding test.

We had the intercom repair meeting in the laundry room at Alder Court on Tuesday morning because the lobby panel had been cutting out and residents were missing deliveries. I was there with Mara Ellis from the building office, Joel Pike from Northline Access, and Mrs. Chen from 4C, who keeps the paper log for the east entrance. The panel still lit up when we arrived, but the sound dropped whenever somebody pressed the silver call button. Joel said the wiring cabinet was dry and the problem seemed to be near the speaker grille, not in the basement power supply. Nobody said the unit was ready, and we did not set a date for closing the repair ticket.

Mara had printed the service notes from the last two visits and put them beside the sign-in sheet. One note said the sound had returned for about an hour after the door closer was adjusted in April. The other said a delivery driver had heard a buzz from the panel but no voice from 4C. Mrs. Chen said she had been home both times and had answered through her kitchen handset. She told us the lobby unit was quieter than that handset, but it was not completely silent. Joel asked us not to press the call button over and over because a loose contact could make the test confusing.

We talked first about forwarding the lobby calls to Mara's office phone while Joel checked the speaker and the cable behind the panel. Mara said, “I can keep the office phone near me until four, but I have a lease appointment at half past two.” Joel said the forwarding setting could be temporary and would not change the numbers stored for individual apartments. Mrs. Chen asked whether the resident handsets would still ring as usual. Joel said they should, and that the test was meant to cover only the lobby call button. He had not tried the temporary setting yet, so nobody treated that as a result.

The office phone sits on a shelf behind the mailboxes, and the signal there is usually steady unless the loading door is open. Mara said that on Tuesdays the parcel carrier often leaves the loading door propped for a few minutes, even though the sign asks drivers to close it. Joel wanted to know whether the phone had to stay at the desk or could be carried to the entrance. Mara said it could be carried, but the charging cord was short and the battery indicator had been blinking since Monday. We agreed to keep the phone at the desk for the first part of the check and to note the time of each lobby call.

Then we went through the work in order. Number one: inspect the grille for lint and paint, without taking the faceplate off. Number two: check the small connector behind the panel and make sure the cable was not pinched against the frame. Number three: use the office phone for forwarding during a single test call, while one person stood in the lobby and another stayed by the desk. Number four: write down whether the sound was clear at both ends, and whether the door closer or the loading door changed anything. Number five: return the setting to normal after the test, unless Mara asked Joel to leave it in place until she had checked with the building manager. Joel said he would bring a narrow screwdriver, a flashlight, and two spare clips, but he did not expect to replace the panel.

Mrs. Chen said she could listen from 4C if the test took place before her afternoon medication delivery. She was not asking for the call to be forwarded to her apartment; she wanted to hear whether her own handset sounded different from the lobby speaker. Mara wrote that distinction in the margin so nobody would mistake it for a request to change her apartment settings. Joel said we could ask her to pick up once, after the lobby test, if she was still home. The delivery usually came between one and two, but the driver had arrived close to noon the previous week, so we left the time flexible.

We also checked what residents had been told. A small notice by the mailboxes said the entrance intercom might be tested, but it did not name a time or say calls could reach the office. Mara said she had not sent a building-wide message because we did not yet know how long the check would take. Mrs. Chen said some residents do not read the paper notices, especially the people who use the west entrance. Joel suggested putting a second notice near that door, and Mara said she could do that after the office phone was free. No one asked residents to leave their doors unlocked, and we did not plan to interrupt calls from apartment handsets.

There was one condition that could affect the afternoon plan. If the lobby door was still locked at six because the evening cleaner had not arrived, Mara said she would not leave the office phone unattended by the entrance. She could keep it at the desk and ask the caretaker, Devon, to stand by the panel for any later test. Devon usually arrived at six fifteen, but Mara had not confirmed his route for that day. Joel said the temporary forwarding could be turned off before he left, and that we should not assume a missed call meant the speaker was fixed or broken. We wrote the condition beside the time notes rather than treating it as a confirmed arrangement.

Before we left the laundry room, Mara read back the notes aloud and asked whether anything important was missing. Mrs. Chen said to include the faint clicking sound she heard after pressing the call button, and Joel added that the click might come from the button itself rather than the speaker. I said the office phone battery and the loading door should both be mentioned, since either could affect what we heard during the test. Mara said, “I will keep the phone on the desk, and I will tell you if I have to leave for my appointment.” The final line on the sheet said the next check would depend on Joel's arrival time and the office schedule. The repair ticket was still open, and we had not recorded a result from the forwarding test.

The rehearsal booking for the North Window quartet is recorded under the name Mara Venn, who reserved Studio B at Alder Street Music Rooms for Saturday, October 19. The session is scheduled from 1:00 to 5:00 p.m., with access to the room beginning at 12:40 for unloading and setup. Mara booked the space after checking the calendar with the other three players, and the reservation confirmation was sent to her by email on September 28. The group expects to use the full four-hour block, although the booking allows them to finish early without changing the fee. The studio address is 44 Alder Street, on the second floor above the bicycle repair shop.

The quartet’s lineup for this rehearsal is Mara on drums, Ivo Chen on electric bass, Nell Ortiz on guitar, and Samir Bell on trumpet. The booking notes list five pieces for the session: “Paper Lanterns,” “Southbound Window,” “Quiet Engine,” “Sunday Map,” and “Borrowed Weather.” Two are new arrangements that have not yet been played together in the room. Mara said, “We need enough time to hear the transitions, not just get through the charts.” The group plans to begin with a short sound check and then work through the pieces in the order listed, returning to any section that needs another pass.

Studio B includes a five-piece drum kit, two guitar amplifiers, a bass amplifier, a keyboard stand, and four music stands. Mara requested the house kit but will bring her own snare, cymbals, kick pedal, and sticks. The kit’s usual configuration has a 22-inch bass drum, two rack toms, one floor tom, and a standard single kick pedal. The room also has a small rug beneath the kit and a separate mat by the entrance for cases. The booking notes say that the house cymbals are not included, so Mara’s cymbals are part of her own equipment rather than a request for studio gear.

Alder Street Music Rooms charges $36 per hour for Studio B, making the listed room total $144 for the four-hour reservation. The group paid a $40 deposit when the booking was made; the remaining $104 is due at the front desk before the session starts. The deposit is credited toward the room charge and is not a separate equipment fee. There is no charge for using the listed house kit or amplifiers. The group has also asked to borrow one extra music stand, which the desk attendant said is available at no additional cost if one is free on the day. That request is noted but is not part of the confirmed room equipment.

The building entrance is beside the bicycle shop, and the music-room door is reached by a short staircase. A lift is available through the rear corridor, but its use has to be arranged with the front desk because the service key is kept there. Mara noted that Samir will bring a trumpet case and a small wheeled bag, while Ivo expects to arrive by bus. Parking is limited to metered spaces on Alder Street, and the closest loading space is usually occupied in the afternoon. The group plans to carry larger cases upstairs unless the rear lift is available. The lift arrangement is optional, not a condition of the booking.

The studio’s access instructions say that the front desk opens at 12:30 p.m. on Saturdays. The group should check in together or have Mara show the confirmation email and settle the balance. If anyone arrives before the desk opens, they must wait in the public entrance rather than enter the rehearsal corridor. The room is reserved only for the stated time, and the next group has a 5:15 p.m. booking, so the quartet needs to clear the room by 5:00. Cases may remain inside during the session but cannot be left there afterward. Mara has written the end time on the group’s shared calendar.

1. Confirm the room and listed equipment at check-in.
2. Pay the remaining $104 before entering Studio B.
3. Keep drinks in closed containers and away from the amplifiers.
4. Return the house kit pieces to their marked positions before leaving.
5. Take all personal instruments and cases out of the building at the end of the booking.

The room-use sheet also asks players to keep the hallway clear and to use the labeled waste and recycling bins near the front desk. The group can move the music stands and chairs during the session, but the furniture must be returned to its usual arrangement before they leave. The drum rug may stay beneath the kit, although the kit itself should not be moved into the storage area. The quartet has no plan to record audio or video, and the booking does not include a recording engineer. Mara asked the others to bring printed charts as well as tablet copies in case the room’s wireless connection is busy.

The studio allows cancellations without losing the deposit when notice is received at least 48 hours before the start time. If the quartet cancels later than that, the deposit is retained, while any payment beyond the deposit is handled according to the desk’s cancellation policy. If the studio has to close unexpectedly, the staff will contact Mara using the phone number on the reservation and offer a new date or explain the refund process. The booking confirmation does not guarantee that the optional extra stand or rear lift will be available. Mara said, “If the lift is in use, we can manage the stairs; the important thing is that we have the room from one until five.”

The reservation is for rehearsal only, not a public performance, and the quartet has not invited an audience. Ivo will bring the printed bass parts, Nell will bring a small pedalboard, and Samir will bring a folding mute holder that can sit beside his stand. The group has agreed to keep the volume moderate during the first ten minutes while they check the room’s balance. No food delivery is planned, and anyone who steps out during the session should tell another player before leaving the building. The confirmation email lists Mara’s mobile number as the day-of contact and gives the front desk number for questions about access, equipment, or payment.

We are setting up the Bell family meal calendar for October because the kitchen whiteboard has become hard to read, and everyone keeps asking what is for dinner. The calendar will cover October 7 through the 20th, and it needs to show who is cooking, who is shopping, and which meals can be moved without wasting food. This is for the six people who eat at the house most nights and for Aunt Celia when she comes over on Sundays. The point is to make the plan easy to check before anyone leaves work, not to make every evening feel fixed.

Start with Monday, October 7. The first meal is chicken and rice with carrots, and the rice should be made in the large blue pot because the small saucepan boils over when we cook for all six. The chicken is already in the freezer in two labeled bags, and one bag is enough for Monday. There should be a green note beside it that says, “Thaw in refrigerator Sunday morning,” since Uncle Dev does not want raw chicken left on the counter. The carrots can be sliced after work, and the leftovers go into shallow containers for lunch the next day.

Tuesday is a no-cook night because Priya has her late library shift and Eli has music lessons from five until six thirty. Leave the vegetable soup in the refrigerator for anyone who wants a bowl, but do not count it as the planned family dinner. Put a reminder under Tuesday to soak the white beans overnight for Wednesday, and write that the bowl with the cracked rim is not for the microwave; it is only for serving cold fruit on the counter. The calendar should also say that the bread from Sunday is in the freezer, not the bread box.

Wednesday, October 9, is bean and squash chili with cornbread, and it can be made in the slow cooker before noon if the beans were soaked the night before. If they were not soaked, use the two cans in the pantry instead, and leave the dried beans for another week. Add shredded cheese at the table because Mara and Lucas like it, but keep the chopped cilantro in a separate dish because Grandpa Leon does not eat it. The cornbread recipe is taped inside the pantry door and calls for a hot oven, so no one should put the paper calendar near the stove.

For Thursday, set out leftover chili for whoever is home early and make a small green salad for dinner. The salad dressing is in the glass jar on the refrigerator door, and the label says “lemon tahini.” Check the date before using it because it was opened last week. Tomas will collect the grocery order at the North Market after his shift on Thursday, and the order number is saved in the family phone note. The bag of pears should stay separate from the onions because the pears are nearly ripe.

Friday is the night for fish tacos with cabbage and black beans, and the fish needs to move from the freezer to the refrigerator on Thursday morning so it can thaw safely. Use the corn tortillas in the top drawer, and warm only what the family needs since they tear if they sit in a stack too long. Write “no cilantro” on Friday because Leon will be at the house, and keep the lime wedges in a covered dish. If Celia comes by, she can bring the green salsa she likes, but the meal should still work without it. Add a note that the leftover cabbage can go into Saturday lunch.

1. Weekend meals. First, Saturday, October 12, is a flexible supper with baked pasta and roasted zucchini. The pasta sauce is already open, so use it before opening the jar in the pantry. The 12th is the school concert, and we will eat sandwiches before it instead, so put baked ziti on Sunday, October 13, and keep Saturday dinner as soup and toast. The school concert begins at six, and the family should leave by five twenty. The soup is in the freezer in a round container marked “tomato,” and it needs to thaw in the refrigerator Friday night.

Sunday is the shared meal with Aunt Celia at one thirty. Put lentil stew and flatbread on the calendar, and ask Celia to bring the small cucumber salad if she is feeling up to it. If she cannot come, the stew still gets made because there is enough for Monday lunch too. Add sliced apples for the children and tea without sugar for Celia. The dining table seats six comfortably, so use the folding chair from the hall closet only if Uncle Dev comes as well, and leave the blue serving spoon beside the stew pot.

2. The following week. Monday, October 14, is a leftovers night, but only if there is at least one full container of lentil stew after Sunday lunch. If the container is less than half full, make scrambled eggs and toast instead, and mark the stew for lunch rather than dinner. On Tuesday the 15th, cook the vegetable lasagna that is in the refrigerator, not the frozen one, because Priya is bringing home a classmate who does not eat meat. Put the ingredients card on the counter so the classmate can check it, and keep the grated Parmesan in its own bowl.

Wednesday, October 16, is pantry pasta with peas and lemon, and Eli can start the water after he gets home at four forty-five. If an adult is not back yet, he should not use the large burner on his own. Tell him to wait in the living room and call his mother instead. The peas are in the freezer door, and the lemon is in the basket beside the kettle. Thursday is still open because Mara has not confirmed her work schedule, so leave a question mark there rather than assigning a meal. The backup is tomato soup and grilled cheese using the loaf labeled “Monday.”

On Friday, October 18, make the turkey meatballs with couscous and green beans. The meatballs are in the lower freezer drawer, and there are two containers. Use only one unless Celia confirms that she is coming over that evening. If the drawer has not been cleared by Wednesday evening, move the green beans to the top freezer shelf so they are not trapped behind the ice packs. If anyone changes a meal, they should tell the others in the group chat before shopping. Well, leave the final square open for Sunday dinner until the review so nobody mistakes a suggestion for a confirmed plan.

The studio is at 18 Alder Court, and the main entrance is the glass door beside the bicycle rack. The loading door is around the alley on the east side, and the keypad there is separate from the one on the front door. Please keep those two codes in different fields because people have been entering the front code at the alley and then calling the caretaker when it does not work. The current front code ends in forty-two, and the loading door code ends in eighty-seven, but I will send both codes through the staff channel rather than put them on the printed list.

The list should start with the people who have regular access and then have a separate section for temporary access. The studio coordinator is Leena Voss, and she keeps the signed paper copy in the blue folder on the middle shelf. The facilities contact is Graham Pike, and he can reset the alley keypad, but only between nine in the morning and five in the afternoon on weekdays. If the keypad fails outside those hours, people should call the building caretaker at the number on the emergency card, not ask Graham to come in after work. The emergency card is taped inside the cabinet door, and the caretaker's name is Oren Bell. His work number, not his personal number, is the one printed there.

Dev Malik is the weekday six o'clock opener, and Iris Vale is the Saturday opener. Iris opens at seven on Saturdays. The door should be checked after each person enters because the latch sometimes catches but does not close all the way. Dev has a brass key for the front entrance and a gray fob for the loading door. Iris has a brass key too, but no loading door fob. If she needs to bring in a large piece on Saturday, she has to ask Leena to borrow the spare fob and return it before she leaves. Do not make a permanent fob for her based on that occasional arrangement.

The regular access names are Dev Malik, Iris Vale, Leena Voss, Graham Pike, and the two print technicians, Suri Bell and Anton Reyes. Suri works Tuesday through Friday, and Anton works Monday through Thursday. They each have access to the print room but not the recording booth because the booth has equipment that belongs to the sound fellows. Suri usually arrives around ten, and Anton starts at eight. Both of them may use the loading door while they are on the schedule. If their shift changes, Leena updates the printed list and the shared spreadsheet together rather than changing one and leaving the other behind. The spreadsheet is called Alder Studio Access, and the current version is in the operations drive under building, then studio, then access.

There are three points to include in a numbered section for temporary access:
1. The visiting ceramic artist Mina Solis can use the main studio from April ninth through April twelfth, from ten in the morning until six in the evening. Mina has a temporary front door code that expires at six on the twelfth and should not be given an alley fob because she is carrying small tools in by hand.
2. The electrician Niko Brand can enter the alley and electrical closet on April tenth between seven and nine in the morning only. Leena will meet him and stay with him while he is inside. His appointment is for the outlet by the wash sink, and he is not cleared to use the rest of the studio.
3. The courier can leave supply boxes inside the front vestibule on April eleventh before noon, but must not be given a code or allowed into the work rooms. Leena or Dev will bring the boxes in after the delivery arrives.

There are two conditions that affect how the temporary entries should be handled. If Mina asks to stay later than six, Leena needs to approve the change first and update both copies of the access list before Mina uses the code after its stated hours. If the electrician's appointment moves to a different morning, Graham has to confirm that he is available to reset the alley code before the new time is added. Otherwise, Niko's original appointment should remain the only time shown. Those limits matter because the front code is shared by several regular users, while the temporary code is assigned to Mina alone, and the alley code is used by the print technicians and the building caretaker.

When we explain the arrangement to people, say, “The printed list shows who is expected in the studio, and the spreadsheet is the place to check whether a temporary visit has changed.” Do not promise that a person has access just because their name appears in an old email. Last month, a former resident named Eli wrote, “The side door always works for me, so I should still be on the list,” but that is not current evidence of permission. Eli's residency ended in January, and Leena has collected the brass key from him. His name should stay off both current access lists, and there is no need to contact him unless he asks about returning a sketchbook that is still in the flat file.

The weekly check should be done on Monday morning. Leena compares the paper list with the spreadsheet and asks Dev to test the front latch. Graham checks the alley keypad during his normal work hours and records whether the buttons respond. Suri checks that the print room names still match the current technician schedule, and Iris checks the Saturday opening note. If a name or time is wrong, the person who notices it should tell Leena rather than write over the paper copy. The blue folder also contains a short form for requesting a new key or a temporary code, and each request needs the person's name, the date needed, the door requested, and the reason for access.

There is one more practical detail for the printed copy. The studio has a narrow entry path, and the fire door must never be propped open while someone carries materials through. If two people arrive together, one person can hold the inner door while the other closes the fire door behind them. The small wheeled cart belongs to the studio and stays beside the sink after use. The folding ramp is stored behind the coat rack, and only Leena or Dev should move it because the lower hinge came loose in March. If someone reports that it is loose again, they should leave it where it is and tell Leena instead of trying to tighten it themselves.

At the bottom of the final list, put the date it was checked and the name of the person who checked it. Do not write the access codes on that copy. The old sheet can be marked superseded and put in the archive envelope in the bottom drawer, but it should not be left beside the current blue folder. The next residency orientation is on April eighth, so the list needs to be ready before that meeting. Leena will bring the folder to the table and explain the difference between the regular names and the temporary entries, and Dev will demonstrate that the front door latch catches properly after it closes.

We are opening registration for the North Quay Autumn Chess Open at the Bellweather Rooms in Alderwick on October 18 and 19 this year. The event is hosted by the Alderwick Chess Circle with help from the Quay Library. The main playing room is Lantern Hall, and the analysis room is upstairs in the Old Map Room. Registration is for over-the-board play only, and the organizers expect a mix of local club members, school players, and visitors from outside the county.

The entry form should ask for each player's full name, federation or club if they have one, rating and rating source if known, age group, contact email, and whether they need a step-free route. Players may leave the club and rating source fields blank, but the email is required for a confirmation and any schedule change. The form should not ask for a home address because the organizers do not need it. Juniors can give a parent or guardian's email instead of their own. The registration page should say that an entry is not confirmed until the fee has been received.

The standard entry fee is £24, and the junior fee is £12. Those amounts include the Friday evening welcome session but not food or travel. The payment reference should be the player's surname followed by NQOPEN. If two players in one household use the same surname, they should add the first initial as well. The treasurer will check bank transfers twice each week and mark the spreadsheet only after the money appears in the account. Cash will be accepted at the library desk on two announced afternoons, and a receipt should be given there. No one should send card details by email.

The advertised entry deadline is October 4, but the organizer wants the form to stay open until October 6 for entries that need an accessibility conversation. After that, the form can take names for a waiting list and should explain that a waiting-list place does not guarantee a board. The player gets a place only if an entrant withdraws and the treasurer confirms the fee. The instruction to the player should be to wait for the confirmation email before paying. People already entered by October 4 should not have to repeat their information when they ask a question.

We need contact names beside the jobs in the volunteer sheet. The coffee table lead is Rhea Bell, and the pairings lead is Mara Venn. Ivo Serrin is the equipment contact. Put Ivo beside the equipment job because he has the spare clocks and knows which boards have loose hinges. Rhea will bring two urns and a box of paper cups, but she needs access to the kitchen by 7:30 on Saturday. The room booking starts at 7:00, and the caretaker has asked us not to prop the outside door open.

The first round is planned for 10:00 on Saturday, with check-in from 8:30 until 9:20. Players who arrive after 9:20 should call the desk rather than assume their place will be held. The director can decide whether a late arrival can join the first round, and no one should promise a bye in advance. There will be five rounds on Saturday and two on Sunday, with a longer lunch break after round three. Pairings will be posted on the board beside the main entrance, and a duplicate will be placed in the analysis room. Players should tell the desk about a result entry that looks wrong before the next round starts.

Say, “Please check your listed rating before the first round and speak to the desk if it needs an update.” Ratings will be taken from the national list downloaded on October 10. If a player has no national rating, the form may record a published club rating with its source written in the notes field. The organizers are not going to estimate a rating from a player's own description. A player who wants to request a rating correction should bring evidence to the director, and the request does not automatically change a pairing already made.

Now the room and access details: the main entrance has three shallow steps, and the side entrance has a ramp. The side door will be unlocked by a volunteer from 8:15 until the start of round one. After that, a player who needs the ramp should call the desk number printed in the confirmation email, and someone will come to let them in. There are two accessible toilets on the ground floor, and reserved seating will be held near the aisle for people who ask for it on the form. The Map Room upstairs is not step-free, so the organizers should send analysis sheets to the main hall if anyone cannot use the stairs.

1. Carry forward each player's name, rating, and payment status from the online form into the registration spreadsheet.
2. Print one check-in list for the desk and a separate list showing only names and clubs for the notice board.
3. Put the clock and board inventory on Ivo's clipboard and ask him to note any missing equipment before doors open.
4. Keep a paper copy of the emergency contact number in the desk folder, but do not display it publicly.

The hall booking includes 48 playing boards and 50 clocks, and the club can borrow 12 more clocks from the Quay Library if they request them by October 8. That request should be made only after Ivo compares the spreadsheet with the inventory. If the final entry count is 60 or more by August 12, reserve the second room at the Bellweather Rooms for the playing overflow. If fewer than 60 players have entered by then, keep the booking to Lantern Hall and do not charge players for the second room unless the organizers separately confirm a change. The venue needs its final table count by October 11, so the number of boards and tables in that message should use the confirmed entries rather than the waiting list.

The welcome session starts at 6:30 on Friday and includes a short explanation of the weekend schedule plus time for players to find their boards. No clock demonstrations are planned during that session because the director is still checking which models are available. A printed schedule should be at the library desk by October 14. The schedule should include the desk phone number, the check-in window, the seven-round plan, and the location of the analysis room. It should also state that players are responsible for arranging their own lunch on Saturday. The library cafe is expected to be open, but that has not been confirmed.

The organizers have asked the library to keep the quiet reading room available for anyone who needs a break from the playing hall. The room is not part of the tournament, and no boards should be set up there. A volunteer should check that the passage to it stays clear and direct questions about the room to the desk rather than making assumptions about its use.

After the last round on Sunday, the director will collect result slips and check that the scores entered on the pairing sheet match them. The desk should keep signed result slips in the blue folder until the treasurer has matched the entry list to the payments. The club plans to send a short event report to the Quay Library during the following week, but the report should wait until the director has verified the final standings. If there is a disagreement about a result, the director should record both players' accounts and leave the result marked for review until it is resolved. The registration team should not announce a final standings list while any result is still under review.

Ich diktiere den neuen Essenskalender für unsere Familie, weil sich seit dem Herbst die Arbeitszeiten geändert haben und wir nicht mehr jeden Abend spontan entscheiden wollen, wer einkauft und wer kocht. Bei uns wohnen meine Schwester Leonie, ihr Sohn Tom und ich in einer Wohnung in Kassel. Meine Mutter Ute kommt meistens am Sonntag dazu, und mein Vater Ralf isst dienstags mit uns, wenn seine Spätschicht endet. Wir haben am Küchentisch besprochen, dass der Kalender nicht wie ein strenger Speiseplan wirken soll, sondern wie eine verlässliche Erinnerung an das, was schon eingekauft ist und wer an dem jeweiligen Tag Zeit hat. Leonie sagte: „Ich möchte morgens sehen, ob ich abends noch zum Sport kann.“ Und Tom meinte: „Dann muss aber auch draufstehen, wenn ich beim Schneiden helfen soll.“ Genau das fand ich sinnvoll, denn er will nicht überrascht werden, wenn er gerade seine Hausaufgaben macht.

Am Samstag haben wir den alten Kalender von der Tür genommen und die Magnete sortiert. Zuerst wollten wir ihn an die schmale Seite des Kühlschranks hängen, denn dort sieht man ihn auch, wenn man den Herd benutzt. Die obere Magnetleiste bleibt für Einkaufszettel frei, und der Kalender beginnt immer am Montag. Ute hat vorgeschlagen, eine Farbe für jede Person zu nehmen. Leonie bekommt Blau, Tom Orange, ich Grün und Ralf Grau. Ute selbst wollte keinen eigenen Farbpunkt, weil sie nicht jede Woche dabei ist. Wenn sie sonntags sicher kommt, trägt sie ihren Namen mit Bleistift ein, und wir machen daraus erst dann einen festen Plan, wenn sie es bis Freitag bestätigt hat.

Für die Woche nach dem nächsten Schulkonzert haben wir die Gerichte gemeinsam gesammelt. Zuerst sollten es sieben warme Essen sein, aber mittwochs sind Tom und ich erst nach halb acht zu Hause, also machen wir an dem Abend Brote und eine Schüssel Salat. Am Montag gibt es Linsensuppe, die Leonie am Sonntag vorkocht. Am Dienstag macht Ralf Kartoffelpfanne mit Paprika und den restlichen Bohnen vom Wochenende. Am Donnerstag ist Nudelauflauf mit Spinat, und am Freitag bestellen wir nichts Festes, sondern essen die Reste, die noch gut sind. Samstags kocht Tom mit mir Pfannkuchen, und sonntags bringt Ute meistens etwas Gebackenes mit. Sie hat diesmal Kartoffelbrot angeboten. Wenn sie es nicht schafft, kaufen wir ein Brot beim Laden an der Haltestelle.

Bei den Einkäufen stehen drei Sachen auf der Liste: erstens Hafermilch, weil Leonie sie für den Kaffee braucht; zweitens zwei Dosen gehackte Tomaten für die Suppe; und drittens ein Bund Petersilie für Ralf. Die Zwiebeln haben wir noch im Korb unter der Treppe, aber vor dem Einkauf muss jemand prüfen, ob dort noch genug sind. Tom fragte, ob er gleich am Montag mit dem Fahrrad zum Markt fahren soll. Ich sagte ja, wenn es nicht regnet und wenn sein Licht am Rad wieder funktioniert. Sonst geht Leonie nach der Arbeit zu Fuß in den kleinen Laden an der Ecke. Sie soll dort keine schweren Flaschen holen, weil sie danach noch ihre Sporttasche trägt. Die Mineralwasserflaschen kaufe ich am Dienstag auf dem Heimweg.

Wir haben auch über Portionen gesprochen, denn die Suppe reicht für vier Schüsseln und wir sind an dem Tag nur zu dritt. Leonie nimmt eine Portion in einem verschlossenen Behälter mit zur Arbeit, und der Rest kommt in den Kühlschrank, nicht ins Tiefkühlfach. Tom isst keine rohen Zwiebeln, und Ralf möchte in seiner Kartoffelpfanne keine Chiliwürfel, obwohl er sonst gern scharf isst. Diese beiden Hinweise schreiben wir direkt neben die Gerichte, damit niemand erst beim Kochen nachfragen muss. Bei der Nudelpackung steht eine ungefähre Menge, aber Tom isst nach dem Training mehr. Deshalb soll Leonie eine zusätzliche Handvoll Nudeln zurücklegen, wenn sie die Tüte öffnet.

Ute hat am Telefon gesagt: „Pois é, domingo funciona, mas só chego depois das seis.“ Das heißt für uns, dass Sonntag grundsätzlich passt, sie aber erst nach sechs kommt. Deshalb essen wir nicht um fünf wie sonst. Wenn Ute später kommt, stellen wir ihr eine Schüssel mit Kartoffelbrot zurück und wärmen die Suppe erst auf, wenn sie angerufen hat. Sie sagte außerdem: „Tá bom, eu levo o pão.“ Also bringt sie das Brot mit. Wir haben das nicht als sichere Zusage für jede Woche verstanden, sondern nur für diesen Sonntag. Wenn sich ihre Rückfahrt ändert, schreibt sie eine Nachricht in die Familiengruppe, und ich ändere den Eintrag.

Unter dem Wochenplan gibt es eine kleine Zeile für Vorbereitungen. Dort steht: am Sonntag Linsen abspülen und in den Topf stellen; am Montag Petersilie waschen; und am Mittwoch Salatgurke schneiden. Die Gurke soll erst am Mittwoch geschnitten werden, damit sie nicht schon am Dienstag trocken wird. Tom hat angeboten, die Magnete nach dem Abwasch zurückzusetzen. Wenn jemand ein Gericht tauscht, muss er den Namen und den neuen Tag ebenfalls verschieben und nicht nur die Farbe ändern. Leonie sagte: „Genau, sonst denken wir beide, der andere kocht“, und klebte einen kleinen Stift an die seitliche Kühlschrankwand, damit die Einträge nicht mit einem Küchenmarker ergänzt werden, der dort nicht mehr schreibt.

Für Krankheit oder unerwartete Schichten gibt es keine festgelegte Ersatzperson. Wir schreiben dann in die Gruppe, was sich geändert hat, und nehmen, wenn möglich, ein Gericht aus dem Fach mit den haltbaren Vorräten. Ralf hat vorgeschlagen, immer eine Packung Reis und eine Dose Bohnen als Reserve zu behalten. Das kam als Vorschlag in den Kalender, aber noch nicht als fester Einkauf, denn wir wollen zuerst zählen, was im Schrank steht. Wenn Tom am Donnerstag länger in der Schule bleiben muss, kocht Leonie den Auflauf schon am Mittwoch und stellt ihn abgedeckt in den Kühlschrank. Dann muss ich ihn nur noch in den Ofen schieben, falls er rechtzeitig abgekühlt ist.

Am Sonntagabend wollen wir kurz prüfen, ob der Plan für die folgende Woche noch stimmt. Dabei schauen wir auf Schichten, Sporttermine und die Vorräte und tragen Änderungen mit Datum ein. Die alten Einträge werden nicht sofort weggewischt, weil Ute manchmal nachfragt, wann wir ein bestimmtes Gericht gekocht haben. Nach zwei Wochen fotografiere ich den Kalender und lösche die abgelaufene Seite erst danach. Dann sammeln wir neue Ideen. Tom möchte im nächsten Monat einmal Gemüsecurry probieren. Leonie hat dazu gesagt, dass sie mitkocht, wenn wir die Schärfe getrennt auf den Tisch stellen. Bis dahin bleibt es nur eine Idee und kein geplanter Termin. Der neue Kalender soll uns entlasten, aber wenn ein Abend anders läuft als gedacht, schreiben wir einfach dazu, was tatsächlich passiert ist.

Hello, this is Nora Bell, and I am trying to arrange weekly cello lessons for my son June at the Harbor Room Music Studio in Westmere. We spoke briefly at the spring student concert, and you said to send the details before asking you to hold a regular time. June is twelve and has played cello for about two years. She reads music comfortably but still needs help changing positions without tightening her left shoulder. She has a school orchestra rehearsal on Wednesday evenings, so that day will not work even if an earlier opening appears.

We are hoping to begin during the week of October 7 and continue through the middle of December, with a break for the week of November 25 because we will be away that week. The first lesson could be Thursday, October 10, after 4:30. She can arrive from school by 4:25 if traffic is ordinary, and I would allow ten minutes to unpack and tune before the lesson. Her father can bring her on most weeks, but I will handle the first visit and any week when he is traveling.

June has a three-quarter-size cello with a soft case, a folding music stand, and a beginner bow. She can bring all of those each week, but the endpin rubber sometimes slips on the studio floor, and I wondered whether the room has a floor anchor or a small mat. She is working on the first movement of the Bréval sonata and a short arrangement of “Greensleeves” from her school book. She would like to keep both pieces in the plan while also learning a few short exercises that address shifting and relaxed bow changes. She is not preparing for an audition, and we are not looking for a performance slot this term.

For the booking record, put Elias Bell as the adult contact and June as the student. Elias is her father, and his mobile is 555-0148. Mine is 555-0193. Please use my number for schedule changes because I answer during the day, and list Elias as the backup contact. His work sometimes prevents him from picking up a call, but he can usually respond to a text by the evening. If you need a second number for a same-day cancellation, you can call him after three.

There are a few practical questions before we settle anything. “The studio page says lessons may be moved with twenty-four hours’ notice, but I could not tell whether that means a credit for a later date or a replacement lesson.” If you can explain the policy, please include it, and also let me know whether the first meeting includes a short parent conversation or whether I should book extra time. June is shy in a new room, and it would help her if she knew beforehand whether I stay for the whole lesson or wait in the hallway. We do not need a long consultation, but I can share her orchestra teacher’s notes if that would make the first lesson more useful.

Here is the schedule information in a numbered section:
1. The preferred weekly time is Thursday at 4:35, and a fifty-minute lesson would be manageable with her homework.
2. If that time is unavailable, please tell me about openings on Monday after five or Saturday between ten and noon before suggesting a different weekday.
3. We can consider a thirty-minute lesson for the first two weeks if that is the only way to get started, but after that we would prefer the regular fifty-minute length.
4. Please say whether tuition is paid monthly or by lesson, and whether the studio charges separately for a missed lesson when notice is given.

We can pay by bank transfer or card and would prefer a monthly invoice sent to nora.bell@fernmail.net. Please do not charge the card automatically unless we have discussed the amount and the billing date first. If a deposit is normally needed, you can tell me the amount and when it is due before we decide about a recurring booking. I have not checked whether the studio lends instruments, so we will bring June’s cello either way, and there is no need to arrange a school pickup. She will come with one of us.

One condition that matters for us is the stair access. June’s cello case is awkward on narrow stairs, and she has a sore ankle that is improving. If the assigned room is upstairs, please let me know before confirming a time so we can check whether she can manage the stairs safely. An available ground-floor room would be easier, but we do not want to assume one is free. If the lesson has to be upstairs, we may still be able to attend provided there is a handrail and we can leave extra time to get settled. Please do not treat the ankle as a request to cancel the lesson; we are only trying to plan the visit sensibly.

Her current orchestra schedule may change after the school posts the winter calendar in early November. If rehearsal is moved to Monday, I will email before accepting any Monday opening, but Thursday should remain clear the whole term. If the school changes its concert date, I will let you know because she may need to miss one lesson that week. At the moment, the concert is expected on December 12, but the school has not confirmed the venue or call time, so we cannot give you a definite absence date yet. We can tell you as soon as the calendar is published.

Please reply with any Thursday availability in the requested period, the lesson length and rate, the cancellation policy, and whether the stairs or room location can be checked before we book. I am not asking you to hold a slot while we consider the details, and a list of possible times is fine. If no Thursday time works, we can compare the Monday and Saturday options with Elias’s travel calendar. I would rather settle the weekly time before sending payment information, and then we can decide whether to start on October 10 or wait for another opening. Thank you for taking a look at all of this, and please address the reply to Nora because I will coordinate the schedule.

We are reviewing the shared-folder sync client for the North Annex archive, and I want the handoff notes to be useful to both the evening desk and the people who maintain the client. I'm speaking this after the Thursday check with Mira Chen and Dev Patel. The folder is called North Annex Field Records. It has about 640 gigabytes in it and is shared by nine staff members across the annex and the records room. The client is version 5.8.2 on the two desk machines and version 5.8.1 on the four loan laptops. The two older laptops are still waiting for their next scheduled update.

Mira said, “The green panel is the one that shows transfer activity on this build,” and Dev said the label stays green even when a transfer is paused, so we should not tell people that the color alone means it is moving. I saw a status line with twelve files waiting and three files actively uploading at 4:18 p.m. on Thursday. That was the count on the North Annex folder, not the whole account. The client had been running for just under two hours by then. The shared folder is set to keep local copies on the desk machines, but the loan laptops use online-only for the archive because their drives have less room.

Please set sync.limit_uploads to eighteen megabytes per minute for North Annex Field Records before the next records scan, and leave the setting for the personal folders unchanged. I am asking for a cap on uploads because the annex has a video review station on the same wireless access point, and Dev measured its connection at twenty-eight megabits per second during the afternoon test. That twenty-eight figure is the measured link speed, not the upload cap. Mira wants the client to pause new uploads when the laptop battery drops below twenty percent, but that is a separate preference, and we have not confirmed that this version supports it. Don't change that preference as part of the upload cap request.

Mira told me, “The folder should finish its first pass overnight if the desk stays signed in, but do not promise that to the scan team.” That was her estimate, not a completion report. The next scan is booked for Friday at 8:30 a.m., and the records team needs the index file available by 8:00 a.m. If the first pass is still running at 7:30 a.m., then message Dev and the records lead before changing any settings. If it has finished by then, leave the client alone and report the completion time in the handoff. The Friday condition matters because the scan uses the index file and should not begin with a partial index. We do not yet know how long the first pass will take on the loan laptops.

For the handoff, list the checks in this order:
1. Confirm that all nine staff still see North Annex Field Records in the shared list, and note which of the six laptops show version 5.8.2.
2. Record the waiting and active file counts with the time of the check, and say whether the count is for this folder or the whole account.
3. Verify that local copy stays selected on both desk machines and online-only stays selected on all four loan laptops.
4. Ask the maintainer to apply the requested eighteen megabytes per minute upload cap to this folder only, and write down when the request is sent. Do not mark the cap as active unless the client actually shows that setting after it is changed.

There are six client machines in the handoff count: two desk machines and four loan laptops. The two older laptops are included in those four, so don't count them as extra machines. We are updating the website for the Lantern Room Reading Club, which meets in the old ferry library in Bellwether. The club started as a monthly gathering in 2018 and now has readers from three nearby neighborhoods. The site should help people find meetings, borrow information about the bookshelves, and learn how to join without making the club sound like a commercial service. Our current pages were built by volunteers, and the new version needs to stay usable on phones because many members check it while they are on the bus.

The home page will have a short welcome, a calendar, and a link to the current reading list. Please keep the welcome under one hundred and twenty words and mention that newcomers may attend two meetings before deciding whether to register. The club does not charge dues, but people can bring a small donation for tea or replacement books. Our treasurer tracks those donations in a notebook and does not want the website to describe them as required fees. The calendar should show both the meeting date and the time doors open because several readers arrive early to talk.

The next meeting is on November twelfth, and we will discuss *The Glass Orchard* by Lena Morrow. The library room opens at six thirty, and the discussion begins at seven. The archive room is booked for Friday afternoon so volunteers can scan the old reading lists. The change is confirmed in the library email, but the scanning session is not open to the public. Please do not imply that visitors can attend. The club discussion is open to registered members and first-time guests, and anyone who needs a quiet place to sit can use the side table near the window as long as they leave the central aisle clear.

On the membership page, visitors should see a simple form with fields for name, email, neighborhood, and an optional note about access needs. We do not need a phone number. The form should say that access notes are shared only with the two meeting hosts and are removed after the season ends. If someone leaves the note blank, the hosts should not contact them to ask for private medical details. Mara will be the access coordinator for questions about the form and website display. She can explain where information goes, but she cannot promise a particular seating arrangement before each meeting.

We have agreed that printed copies of the reading list will be available at the library desk, and the online version should include author names, publication years, and a short description of each title. Please do not add ratings because the club has not voted on a rating system this season. People can suggest future books through a separate suggestion box, which is checked at the last meeting of each month. The club currently has twenty-four members, and the list should not present that number as a limit since attendance changes from month to month. The small-print edition should use dark text on a cream background, and the phone view should not rely on color alone to distinguish past meetings from upcoming ones.

1. For the events section, show the next discussion with the title and author, show when doors open and when the conversation begins, and include the library room name.
2. Include the following club note: “We try to make room for careful disagreement, and nobody has to finish a book to join the conversation.”
3. Link to the reading list and the guest information form, but do not place the donation note beside the form because new visitors have mistaken it for a payment step before. The list page also needs a plain-text version for members who print from the library computer.

If a meeting is moved because the library closes unexpectedly, the two hosts will update the calendar and put a notice on the home page before sending an email. The site should not claim that email is the only way to receive an update because some members do not use email. When a change is made after noon on meeting day, the hosts will also phone guests who have asked for a call back and have provided a number for that purpose. Otherwise, the public calendar is the source to check.

People have asked whether the club will record discussions. The answer is no. Meetings are not recorded, and the site should explain that members may quote a published passage for discussion but should not upload photographs of another attendee without permission. One reader said, “I like hearing different readings of the same page, but I do not want my face on a public site.” The quote can appear on the welcome page without identifying the speaker.

The volunteer team is planning a small launch in early December, but no exact launch day has been selected. Before then, we need to check that the calendar works with a screen reader, confirm that the form sends access notes only to the hosts, and make sure the older reading lists still open from the archive page. If the tests find a problem, the launch should wait until the issue is fixed. The club can continue using its existing notice board while the website is being checked, and no one should promise members that every archive item will be available on launch day.

At the bottom of the about page, include the library address as 14 Quay Lane, Bellwether, and say that the number 6 bus stops across the street. Bicycle racks are beside the side entrance, and the main entrance has three steps with a handrail. Visitors who need a step-free route should email Mara before the meeting so a host can meet them at the garden entrance. The garden entrance is unlocked only during scheduled club hours and is not a general library entrance.

Finish with a contact line for the two hosts using hosts@lanternroom.org, and state that messages are normally answered within three days during the reading season. Outside the season, replies may take longer. Do not describe the hosts as librarians because they are club volunteers and the library staff are not responsible for membership questions. The page should end with the next scheduled date once it is confirmed and should not show a placeholder date as if the club had already announced it.

Hello, this is Neri Sol from Blue Reed Ceramics, calling about the delivery to the Alder Street Arts Center for Thursday morning. I want to get the route and receiving notes into one place because we have two kilns sending work, and the building has a few access details that are easy to miss. The order is for the spring studio exhibition, and it includes thirty-six bowls, twelve tall vases, and eight shallow wall panels. The pieces are packed in nine wooden crates with foam corners, and each crate has a paper inventory sleeve taped inside the lid.

We are loading at the Blue Reed workshop on West Quarry Road. The truck should leave at 6:45 and reach Alder Street around 8:15 if the bridge traffic stays normal. The driver is Elian Cross, and the second crew member is Jo Park. They have delivered to the center before, but not through the north entrance. This time, the north entrance is blocked for electrical work, so use the courtyard gate on Pike Lane. The gate is usually locked before eight, and the center asked us to call the front desk when we are two minutes away so someone can release it.

For the receiving contact, Priya Sen is the receiving supervisor, and she will sign the condition sheet. Lio Merritt is the inventory clerk and does not sign the delivery. Priya can be reached through the center desk at 555 0186 if she is away from the loading room. The desk should not sign in her place. The driver can wait beside the covered courtyard wall for up to fifteen minutes while they locate her. After that, call me before unloading anywhere else.

There is a narrow turn between the gate and the loading bay, so the truck should stop at the painted blue square, and the crew should bring the crates through the double doors one at a time. The doorway measures just under one meter across, and the panels need to stay upright the whole route from truck to gallery. The route has a rubber floor runner, but there is a small metal lip at the threshold. Jo has a folding ramp in the van and should set it over the lip before the first crate comes inside. The ramp was checked yesterday, and both straps are intact.

Section 1: Receiving checks.
1. Compare the labels against the paper inventory and count all nine crates before anyone signs.
2. Photograph the outside of each crate from two sides and note any fresh dents or wet marks.
3. Open only crate four because it contains the sample bowl that the curator asked to inspect before the rest are placed. The sample is wrapped in blue tissue, and the packing note is tucked under the top foam. If the bowl has a crack or the tissue is wet, leave it in the crate and call me before opening any other crate.

When the center confirmed the booking, their coordinator said, “Please keep the gallery doors clear until the curator has checked the tall pieces.” That means the crates can be staged along the west wall, but not in the doorway. The gallery floor was refinished last week, and the center wants clean wheels on the cart. There are clean covers in the side pocket of the van. Use those covers rather than the old felt pads because the pads have clay dust on them. The crew can use the center hand truck only after asking the front desk, since it may be reserved for the exhibition panels.

Weather is the main concern for the outdoor part of the route. The forecast shows a chance of showers after seven. If rain starts before the truck leaves the quarry, the crew must add the waterproof top sheet and wait under the workshop awning until the rain eases. If rain begins after departure, call the center desk and use the covered courtyard wall for unloading. Do not leave a crate on the pavement, even for a short time. The sheet is in the narrow compartment behind the passenger seat, and the straps are marked with yellow tape. If the route is dry, the sheet can stay packed.

Section 2: After the first inspection, place the bowls on the low padded trolley and keep the vases in their crates until Priya has checked the labels. The wall panels travel flat only inside their foam trays and should be carried by two people. Do not lean them against the gallery wall because the new paint is still curing. Elian should keep the delivery receipt and the signed condition sheet in the clear pouch on the dashboard. Jo should send me three photos of the staged crates and one photo of the signed sheet before the truck leaves the courtyard. If phone reception is poor, the photos can be sent from the workshop after the return trip.

The center expects its curator at nine and the exhibition installer at 9:30, so the delivery needs to be fully checked before the installer begins laying out the room. If there is a delay at the gate, tell the front desk whether it is the electrical closure or the missing key, and give them the updated arrival estimate. Do not promise a new time until Elian has checked traffic. Once the crates are inside, call me with the count and any damage notes, even if everything looks fine. Then leave the signed original with Priya and bring the duplicate receipt back to the workshop.
