We got the delivery for the Willow Market stall on Saturday, the twelfth of October, and I want to get down what happened while the timing is still clear. The stall is run by Mara Ellis and her brother Jonah, and they sell apples, pears, plum jam, and the small bags of dried herbs. The produce came from two farms outside Bellmere, and the jam was made in the kitchen behind the old mill. The morning was cold but dry, and the market manager had asked everyone to keep the lane beside the fountain open because a repair crew was bringing a pump through at 10:30.

Our van left the west depot at 6:40 with 32 apple crates, 12 pear crates, and six insulated boxes of jam and herbs. The stall steward was supposed to meet the van at the north gate and guide it to the loading space. The driver was still responsible for checking the seal and counting the boxes before anyone signed the sheet. The driver was Calvin Reed, and he called Mara at 7:12 to say the bridge near Alder Road was moving slowly. He did not say that the van would be late. He said he would call again if the delay changed the arrival time.

Mara and Jonah had reached the market at seven and set out the folding tables under the blue canvas cover. One table was for fruit, and the shorter table was for jam and herbs. They kept the price cards in a tin because a gust had blown them down the week before. Beside the stall, they left a clear route for the repair crew and put two empty baskets near the corner for customers to return jars. Mara said, “If the pump team needs the lane, we can shift the baskets, but nobody should move the apple crates without asking.” She was talking about the narrow passage, not the whole stall, and Jonah agreed to watch that side while she checked the delivery list.

Now, the numbered handover notes:
1. The van should use the north gate and park in the marked loading space, not beside the fountain.
2. The steward should count the fruit crates with Jonah and compare the totals to the printed sheet.
3. The insulated boxes should stay closed until the shade cloth is ready, because the jam can soften in direct sun.
4. If the repair crew arrives before unloading is finished, they get the clear lane first, and the stall team waits with the van out of the way.
5. Any damaged fruit goes in the blue return crate, and Mara needs a photo before the driver leaves.

At 7:38, Calvin called again and said the bridge had cleared, but a delivery cart was blocking the last turn into the market. The market manager sent a volunteer named Priya to the north gate to point the van toward the loading space. Calvin arrived at 8:05 and stopped where the painted sign said “Deliveries Only.” Mara was checking a list with the bakery next door, so Jonah met Priya and Calvin at the gate. The seal was intact, and the count matched the sheet, except one apple crate had a split corner. Calvin said, “It stayed level, and nothing has fallen out.” Jonah took a photo of the corner before moving it.

When the boxes reached the stall, Jonah put the pears on the lower shelf and the apples in rows by size. Mara opened one insulated box only after the canvas shade was tied down. The jam jars were cool, and there was no leak. The herb bags had dry labels, and the paper around them was not torn. The damaged apple crate held fruit that looked sound, but Mara kept it separate until she had checked the bottom layer. She asked Calvin to stay for the final count, and he waited by the marked space rather than blocking the route. The repair crew arrived at 8:32 and rolled the pump through without asking the stall team to move anything.

Well, the final count was 31 full apple crates and one damaged crate, 12 pear crates, six jam boxes, and two herb bundles packed inside the last box. The printed sheet listed the herb bundles as separate pieces, so Mara wrote a note beside that line rather than changing the delivery total. She sent the photo of the split crate to the farm by text and asked whether they wanted it returned with the empty jars. Calvin signed the sheet after Jonah read the totals aloud, and Mara gave him the yellow copy. The farm replied that the fruit could stay at the stall and asked for the crate to come back on the next scheduled run.

By 9:15, the lane was clear, and the stall was ready for customers. The repair crew had finished with the pump, and the market manager said the fountain side could open again. Jonah moved the return baskets beside the jam table, and Mara put out a small card explaining that customers could bring clean jars back for a discount. A woman who buys herbs every week asked whether the rosemary was from the same farm as last month, and Mara said it was from the south field this time. She did not promise that next week's batch would be the same because the farm had not confirmed what they would harvest.

The damaged apple crate stayed underneath the table with the photo and the farm's message clipped to the delivery sheet. Mara said they should not sell from that crate until she had checked every piece in daylight, and Jonah agreed to sort it after the morning rush. If the fruit underneath was bruised, they would put it in the return box; otherwise, they would move it into the regular apple rows. The van left at 9:21 with the empty insulated boxes, and the yellow copy of the sheet remained in the stall tin. The main thing for next Saturday is to check whether the farm has changed the herb bundle count before printing the new list and to keep the north gate handover in place.

I am forwarding the exchange packet for the North Quay to Bellmere train booking because the travelers need to compare the replacement seats with the original tickets before the station desk closes on Thursday. The booking belongs to Lena Vos and her brother Arin, and the journey is set for the twenty-third of October. They are leaving from North Quay at 16:20 and changing at Alder Junction after a twelve-minute connection. Their original seats are coach four, seats 18 and 19, and the exchange screen now shows coach six, seats 31 and 32. I checked the names against both passports, and the spelling matches.

The reason for the exchange is that Lena has a folding mobility frame, and the original carriage has a narrow entrance. The station agent at North Quay said that the new carriage has a level boarding point beside platform three, but she asked us to verify that detail with the staff at Alder Junction before the tickets are collected. I am forwarding the packet to Joel at the travel desk and copying Lena so she can see what is still pending. The fare difference is eleven pounds and forty pence for both passengers, and the payment receipt is attached under the booking reference NQ 58417.

Lena told me that she can travel on the later service if the level boarding point is unavailable, but Arin has to reach Bellmere before seven for a scheduled appointment. They do not want separate trains, and they have not agreed to cancel the trip. The replacement service leaves North Quay at 17:05 and arrives at Bellmere at 19:26. The earlier service remains available at 16:20 if the original carriage can take the frame. The station desk closes at 18:00, and the telephone line is open until 20:30, so there is time to ask about boarding before anyone collects the new tickets.

When I spoke with the desk clerk called Mara, she said the exchange is held temporarily and not yet issued. She said the hold lasts until noon on Monday and that the printed tickets can be collected from any staffed station once the desk confirms the carriage detail. I wrote down her words: “We can keep the seats on hold until Monday, but the frame must fit through the accessible entrance before the exchange becomes final.” She also said not to use the kiosk because it cannot display the boarding note. I have kept the original tickets in the blue folder and have not handed them to the carrier.

The documents in the packet are these: 1. The original booking confirmation with both passenger names and the 16:20 departure. 2. The exchange quotation with the new 17:05 service and the fare difference. 3. The payment receipt showing the card ending in 6042. And 4. The message from Alder Junction asking for the frame width. The message gives a maximum doorway width of 71 centimetres, and Lena measured the folded frame at 68 centimetres with the side clips removed. The frame is 74 centimetres wide with the clips in place, so the clips have to be taken off before boarding.

I am including the measurement because the condition matters for the booking. If the frame without its side clips is accepted at Alder Junction, then Lena and Arin can use the replacement seats together and keep the later service. If the station staff say the frame must go through with the clips attached, then the present measurement is too wide, and we need to ask whether the original train can accommodate it. Neither answer has come in yet. Joel should check with the station before the hold expires and should leave the exchange unissued while the boarding question remains open.

The message from Alder Junction also says that passengers should report to the platform assistance point twenty minutes before departure and give the conductor the booking reference. The assistance point is beside the red timetable case near the east entrance. Lena has asked whether one person can wait with the frame while the other carries the bags, and I have told her that the staff have not answered that question. The bags are one small case each, and the frame folds down to a length of 83 centimetres when the clips are removed.

There are two practical details for the travel desk. The first is that the North Quay lift will be out of service from 15:00 until 16:00 on the day of travel, and the station notice directs passengers to the west entrance. The second is that the footbridge at Alder Junction has a short ramp but no lift, according to the reply from the station. The staff may be able to arrange a platform crossing if they know about it in advance. Lena can manage three steps with a handrail, but she cannot carry the folded frame while stepping, so the boarding arrangement and the connection need to be discussed together.

Please keep this complete packet with the booking record and forward the station reply to both travelers when it arrives. The exchange quotation expires at noon on Monday, and the original tickets remain valid until the desk issues a replacement. Lena asked me not to promise that the later train is suitable until the doorway measurement has been checked, and Arin said he will keep the appointment details flexible for now. If there is no reply from Alder Junction by Monday morning, Joel can call the assistance desk and note the answer without issuing the exchange. The blue folder is in the locked drawer at reception, and the booking reference is written on its front.

output:
We received the concert subtitle file from the Harbor Hall on Monday morning, and I opened the version that Jo Leung had exported after the late set. The file is called *Winter Room Final.srt*, but the word “final” is just part of the filename; it is not the approved delivery. The recording covers the full concert, from the doors opening through the last announcement, and the house microphone is separate from the feed sent to the stage cameras. I listened to both because the first draft puts several audience answers under the singer’s lines, and the room microphone makes those answers much clearer than the camera feed.

The first issue is the welcome at the start of the recording. Mara says, “Good evening to everyone who found us through the rain,” and the crowd answers, “You too.” The draft has “you two,” which makes the reply look like a reference to two people. When Mara asked whether that answer should stay, I said, “Well, yes, leave it in,” because the audience is answering her directly and the moment is audible on both recordings. She also says, “There are spare programs by the door,” and the draft leaves out “spare.” That word matters because there are no programs at every seat, and the subtitle should not promise that there are.

I made a listening copy with timecode notes but did not change the exported file. The difference matters because Jo is still comparing the earlier text against the live recording on her laptop. We agreed to keep one working copy in the shared folder and to put review notes in a separate document. The file was delivered at a slightly different frame rate from the camera picture, so the subtitles begin about half a second early near the first song. I can align them after the transcription is settled, but I have not done that yet. If the final camera reference arrives before the sound check on Wednesday, I will use that reference for timing; otherwise, I will leave the timing notes attached and ask Mara which picture she wants us to use. The wording can be reviewed without deciding that question.

During the quiet introduction, the cellist says the German word *er* and then points toward the balcony. The note from the interpreter says *er* means “he” here because she is referring to the stage manager, who has just crossed the balcony, not to the cellist. The next phrase is *um halb acht*, and in this sentence *um* means “around,” so the spoken meaning is “around half past seven,” not a hesitation or a request to wait. One of the volunteers suggested deleting both words because they looked like filler in the rough subtitle, but they carry different meanings. The German line is part of the introduction and should remain in German, with an English subtitle that gives the intended sense. The interpreter has not asked us to add a pronunciation guide.

The percussionist also says *tá tudo bem* when he checks with the sound desk before the first song. The phrase is colloquial Portuguese and means “everything is okay” in that exchange; it is an answer to a question about the monitor mix, not a general announcement to the audience. The sound desk engineer replies, “Yes, the left wedge is clear,” and the percussionist nods. The old subtitle says “everything was fine,” which changes the present check into a past report. Use “everything is okay” unless Mara requests a closer conversational translation. We should not add a speaker label because the camera does not show who is speaking, but the timing and the reply make the exchange clear.

Numbered section: Checks before export
1. Compare each subtitle line with the clean room microphone and mark any word that is masked by applause. Do not fill a gap from the printed program alone.
2. Check the singer names against the running order. Jo has the name of the guest violinist as Elian Voss, but the printed card says Elian Vos, and the artist’s own site uses Voss, so leave Voss in the file until Mara confirms which spelling she booked.
3. Review the audience lines for speaker changes and keep the short replies when they answer a spoken question.
4. Check that every subtitle stays on screen long enough to read. The song titles have their own style sheet and should not be changed to sentence case just to match the spoken dialogue.

After the interval, Mara introduces the next piece as “a song from my first winter at the Harbor Hall.” The recording sounds like “first winter,” not “fifth winter,” and Jo’s note says the singer mentioned the year in an interview. I checked that interview, and she says she first played the hall in 2019, but she does not give a winter number, so the subtitle should follow what is audible and say “first winter.” Do not change it to the year from the interview. The two sources can both be accurate without saying the same thing. The next line is partly covered by a cough, and the words after “tonight” are not clear. I marked the timecode for review instead of guessing from the lyrics sheet.

At the end of the concert, the venue manager says, “Thank you for staying while we reset the room,” and then asks people to take the blue route out because the east doors are closed. The draft subtitle says “blue roots,” which is an automatic caption error. The printed safety sign says “blue route” singular, and the manager points to the blue arrows on the wall. Keep the instruction as spoken, and do not add that the east doors are locked because she only says they are closed. The condition for changing that line is a clear second recording of the announcement from the foyer microphone. If it confirms the same words, Jo can replace the marked line before the camera timing pass. If it does not arrive by Thursday morning, the timecode note should remain, and the uncertain words should not be presented as certain.

I have left the closing applause in the subtitle file because the audience keeps clapping under the final exchange, and the recording does not cut away until the lights come up. There is no spoken encore request on either microphone, although the stage manager’s notes mention that some people called for one outside the room. Those notes are not part of the concert audio and should not be used to add a line. The last audible sentence is Mara saying, “Take care on your way home.” The word “home” is clear even though the applause starts before she finishes the sentence. The final subtitle can stay on screen through the end of her voice, and the file should then end on the actual fade of the room microphone rather than an added closing card.

The studio is in the old ferry warehouse on Birch Lane, and the entrance is the blue door beside the loading bay. The list is not a record of who owns a key; it shows who may enter and which rooms they can use. Please keep that distinction clear, because the building manager checks the access list against the alarm log every Friday afternoon, and he has asked us not to leave old permissions in place just because somebody still has a brass key.

On the current sheet there are twenty-three names and four people who have left the cooperative. Last spring, we added the ceramics room and the quiet edit room, so the room column needs to stay beside each name rather than moving into a note at the bottom. Please spell the new platform TideBoard exactly like that, because the invite will point to its access page. We are still using the paper copy clipped inside the front cupboard as a backup, and the copy should show the date it was checked, the person who checked it, and the next review date.

For the new group, we have six members and one visiting tutor. The tutor can enter the main studio and the wash-up room, but not the equipment cage unless a staff member is present. The cage has the large paper cutter and the spare drying racks, and the insurance note says a visitor cannot be left alone in there. The group is booked Tuesday and Thursday evenings from six until nine, and they can arrive fifteen minutes early to set up, but they should not use the space before five forty-five even if the outside door happens to be unlocked.

For the weekend keyholder, put Ivo as weekend keyholder. Mara is coordinating the open day, but she is not carrying the alarm fob. Ivo has agreed to lock up on Saturday and Sunday this month, and his access should include the main studio, the wash-up room, and the front cupboard, but not the office. The alarm fob stays in a numbered envelope in the cupboard when it is not with him. On Monday morning, he will return it to the envelope and text me that the cupboard is locked.

4. Jo can use the wash-up room during the community class on the twenty-sixth, but should not be given a standing permission after that evening.

This is the dye log for the second week of October at the north room vats at Linden Mill, and I am dictating the entries after the evening check. The room was twenty-one degrees at seven in the morning and twenty-four at the last reading. The hygrometer near the west door showed sixty-eight percent, and the small fan stayed off because the cloth on the drying rail was still damp.

On Monday, Mara Vellum weighed twelve kilos of undyed wool from bale forty-six and marked the lot as W-46-B. The wool had a little more lanolin than the sample from Friday, so she used the rinse tank for nine minutes instead of seven. She wrote that the water looked cloudy but not brown, and she did not change the bath recipe. The rinse was recorded at thirty-eight degrees, and the wool was turned twice by hand.

I asked Mara whether she had checked the scale before weighing, and she said, “Well, yes.” The brass weight was still on the hook beside the scale, and she had tested zero with the empty tray before she started. That “well” is her answer, not a hesitation. The small notebook does not show a second scale check after lunch, and the log should not imply one.

On Tuesday, the indigo vat was prepared with four hundred grams of leaf powder and three hundred milliliters of lime water at nine fifteen. The mixture stood for forty minutes before the first dip. Jonas Rehn dipped six skeins from lot W-46-B for three minutes each and left them exposed to air for twelve minutes. He wrote that the first skein appeared pale blue and the sixth looked more even, but he was unsure whether the difference came from the tying or from the vat. The temperature went from twenty-nine degrees before dipping to thirty-one degrees at the end. The pH strip read nine point four. Jonas said, “Do not call the batch finished until the skeins are dry, because the shade can deepen as they lose moisture.”

On Wednesday, the blue cloth was dry by ten thirty, and Mara entered the shade as medium blue on the mill card. The matching card number is Indigo 7C. She compared the first and sixth skeins again beside the north window and kept the note that the sixth looked more even. She did not change the shade entry. She cut a small sample from the loose end of each skein and put both samples in envelope twelve. The envelope is in drawer three under the cards from September. A thread came loose on the fourth skein and was tied back before the sample was cut. Nobody recorded any loss of yarn.

On Thursday, the madder pot was set up for the rust-colored wool from lot R-19. The recipe card calls for six hundred grams of madder root and two liters of water for every ten kilos of wool. This lot weighed eight kilos, so Mara used four hundred and eighty grams of root and one point six liters of water. She kept the pot at seventy-two degrees for fifty minutes and stirred every ten minutes. The water was not allowed to boil because the card says boiling may make the color dull. At the end, the wool looked orange in the pot and rust-colored after rinsing. Mara marked that change as an observation rather than a final shade result.

On Friday, the rinse water from lot R-19 was clear by the third change, but the wool still smelled faintly of madder at noon. Mara moved it to the drying rail on the east wall, where there was more space. She left a note to compare the shade after it had dried fully. The rail was not near the window so that the afternoon sun would not fall on the sample bags. The final reading in the room was twenty-three degrees and sixty-two percent humidity. A bucket with a cracked handle was removed from the floor and placed beside the repair bench. It was not used for dye or rinse water.

There is a conversation note from Luis Ferreira, who was carrying the sealed jar of indigo reserve back to the cupboard. He said, “Tá bom, I will put it on the upper shelf and write the date on the lid.” The jar label reads “Reserve Indigo October Eleven,” and the cupboard record says the lid was checked at four forty. The phrase “tá bom” means “okay” in his note and is not a batch rating.

1. Storage and follow-up
   1. Keep the two indigo samples in envelope twelve until Mara compares them with the dry skeins.
   2. If the rust-colored wool is still damp on Monday, leave the shade field blank and repeat the comparison later. Do not enter a final shade from the orange appearance in the pot.
   3. Return the sealed reserve jar to the cupboard after checking that the lid date can still be read. The reserve was not opened this week, and there is no record of how much remains.
   4. If the pH meter is available before the next indigo batch, compare it with the paper strip because Jonas used the strip reading for this entry. No meter result is recorded.

At the bottom of the page, Jonas copied a message from the visiting dyer, Frau Keller. She wrote, “Er kommt um sechs”—“He comes at six.” If he is coming at six, keep the east doorway clear until then. The German note does not identify who he is. The log does not say that anyone arrived that evening, so keep the message as a note and do not add an arrival time. The doorway was clear at the seven o'clock room check, and the wool on the east rail was still damp.

The next entry should begin with the Monday morning inspection and should record the dryness of lot R-19 before anyone decides whether to fill in its shade. The indigo samples remain in drawer three, and the reserve jar stays sealed in the upper cupboard. The cracked bucket remains beside the repair bench pending a new handle. The final page should include the room readings and the note that no final shade was entered for the madder wool.

output:
This fall, the Lantern College Film Society is building a program around movies made in small towns and the way public places change when people move away. We have forty-three active members on the mailing list and twelve people who have volunteered for at least one shift. Our usual meetings are in the media lab on Tuesdays, but the lab is booked for a photography class on October 8, so we are meeting in the library seminar room that night. The room has a screen but no speakers, and Professor Elian said we can borrow the portable set from the language department if we return it before noon on Wednesday. We are keeping the program open to students and staff, and guests will need to sign in at the front desk.

The opening film is a fictional documentary called *The Mile Marker*, about a family-run diner beside a highway that was rerouted in 1986. The filmmaker has emailed a permission letter for one campus screening, and the society has to send the final date and room before the letter is complete. Our second choice is a comedy called *June at the Depot*, which follows two cousins trying to keep a town train station open as a community space. We have not heard back from that director yet, so it stays a backup rather than a confirmed title. Leah found a short film by an alum named Oren Vale that could fit before either feature, but it is only nine minutes and has captions in English and Spanish. She wants to ask whether the filmmaker would join us by video for a question period.

At Monday's planning meeting, we looked at the old poster template and agreed the society name should be bigger than the film titles because people kept reading the date but missing who was presenting. Niko was assigned the projection coordinator role, and Lale was assigned treasurer, so the equipment receipts go to Lale and the projector checklist goes to Niko. Our secretary, Imani, will update the shared calendar after we confirm the room. She has marked October 15 as a possible date for the first screening, not a final booking, because the student union has not sent its fall events list. She said, “I can hold the evening on our calendar, but I cannot promise the auditorium until the union checks for a conflict.”

The society has a small budget of six hundred and eighty dollars from its student activities allocation. Ninety dollars is already set aside for captioning two older films, and the print shop quoted one dollar and twenty cents per color poster if we order at least thirty. We have fourteen folding display stands in the equipment closet, although two have cracked feet and should not go near the stairwell. The library can lend us a table for the lobby, but we need to request it three business days ahead. Last spring, some guests waited outside the wrong entrance because our signs pointed toward the loading door, so this time we want one sign at the courtyard gate and another beside the accessible entrance.

We also want the program to feel welcoming to people who do not know much about film discussion. Jules suggested giving each guest a card with two questions, one about a detail they noticed and one about how the setting shaped the story. Dev said the cards should not ask people to explain what a film means, since that can sound like there is only one correct answer. At the last meeting, Mina brought a map of the neighborhood around the old Rialto cinema and showed where the bus stops moved after the street redesign. The map might be useful for the lobby display, but we need permission from the local history archive before we reproduce it. Mina has the archivist's email and plans to ask about a low-resolution copy for one evening.

1. Confirm the room and screening date with the student union and send the filmmaker the details.
2. Ask the language department about borrowing the speakers and write the return time on the equipment sheet.
3. Get an estimate from the print shop for thirty posters and check whether they can deliver them to the media lab.
4. Ask Oren Vale if he is available for a video question period and whether the short has a separate caption file.
5. Make a new projector checklist and put the contact number for campus support at the top.

Those are tasks for the committee before the next Tuesday meeting, and Imani said she can circulate the list on Monday morning.

If the weather service predicts heavy rain by noon on the screening day, we should move the courtyard welcome table inside the library entrance and ask two volunteers to guide people from the bus stop. If the forecast is clear, the table can stay by the courtyard gate, but we still need to keep the accessible entrance unobstructed. This condition matters because the library has only one indoor lobby table and another student group may reserve it. We should not print the welcome signs until the room is confirmed, so the location line does not have to be covered with tape.

At the next meeting, we will compare the available dates with the union calendar and decide whether *The Mile Marker* can be the opening film or whether *June at the Depot* should remain the first option. Nobody has chosen a final film yet. Lale will bring the budget sheet, and Niko will bring the projector checklist with the speaker cable lengths written down. The society can invite the history archive after we know whether the map may be displayed, and we can ask the filmmaker about a video visit once the date is firm. Imani wants to leave ten minutes at the end of the meeting for members to raise other ideas, including a possible spring workshop on making captions. She said we should write down questions even if we cannot answer them that night, so the next program does not depend on one person's memory.

output:
Last Thursday, our household was expecting a parcel with two replacement hinges and a small box of screws for the pantry door, and my sister Mara was going to be home, but her bus route changed, so I took the pickup instead. The delivery notice said the driver would arrive sometime between one and four, and that an adult had to show photo identification because the parcel needed a signature. I moved my afternoon call to the kitchen table and put my keys and wallet beside the blue bowl by the front door so I would not have to look for them later.

At about twelve forty, the tracking page changed to “out for delivery” and showed six stops ahead of ours. I checked that the building entrance was not blocked because a plumber had left a toolbox near the stairs, and I shifted it against the wall. The parcel was addressed to Mara Salcedo at 18 Alder Row, and our buzzer label still said Salcedo even though the landlord had asked us to add my name. I had not done that yet. The notice also showed a note from the sender saying “keep upright,” which mattered because the hinge parts were packed in a narrow cardboard sleeve that could bend if someone pushed it under the door.

My neighbor Joana came out carrying a folded laundry basket while I was checking the notice and asked if I was waiting for the parcel. I said, “Right, that’s the one,” and she offered to keep an eye out from the landing while she sorted her laundry. She is usually home during lunch and can hear the downstairs bell from her flat. She said, “Beleza, I can listen, but I have to take a call at one thirty.” I thanked her and said that was plenty because the tracking estimate had not narrowed yet. Joana put the basket beside her door and left the hall clear so the courier could turn around with a trolley.

The driver rang the bell shortly after two and asked through the intercom, “Are you the person at number eighteen?” I said, “Yes, this is Mara’s brother Daniel, and I can show my identification.” He said, “The label has Salcedo, but the name on the buzzer is hard to read, so I will check it at the door.” I brought my wallet and opened the main entrance but kept the apartment door on its chain while I looked through the side window. His jacket had the parcel company logo, and he held a handheld scanner. He said in German, “Er kommt um halb drei,” when he looked at his route screen. Then he switched back to English and explained that the next scheduled stop was at half past two. I asked whether he meant our parcel or the next one, and he pointed to our address on the screen, so I understood he meant ours.

1. I showed him my photo card, and he compared the street number and surname with the label, then asked me to say the recipient’s full name. I said Mara Salcedo and spelled Salcedo slowly.
2. He looked at the sleeve and asked whether it was fragile. I said the sender’s note says “keep upright” and showed him the side where the instruction was printed.
3. He scanned the parcel, but the first scan did not register, and he tried again after turning the screen toward the window.
4. I signed with my usual short signature and checked that the screen displayed Daniel Salcedo rather than Mara because I was the person accepting it. He handed me the parcel and said, “Please do not leave it in the hallway because the building entrance is shared.”

Before he left, I asked what would happen if I had not been at home. He said, “If nobody answered, I would take the parcel back to the van and leave a card with a collection point and a new pickup window.” He added that the sender had selected “signature required,” so he could not put it behind the recycling bins even if I gave permission over the phone. I asked if Joana could sign for it on another day, and he said only if the delivery account allowed an alternate recipient and the name was entered before the next attempt. I said, “Okay, that makes sense,” and he confirmed that this parcel had now been signed for in person, not left with a neighbor.

Once he had gone, I carried the box inside and set it upright on the kitchen floor rather than on the counter because the screws were loose inside the sleeve. Mara messaged me asking whether it had arrived, and I replied, “Yes, the parcel is here, and I signed for it.” She asked whether the package looked crushed. I checked both ends and told her the cardboard was slightly creased near one corner, but the paper seal was unbroken. Joana called from the landing to ask if the driver had needed help with the trolley. I said no, but thanked her for listening for the bell. She laughed and said she had finished her call just before he arrived.

Mara got home at six and compared the label with the order on her phone. The hinges were the correct size, and all eight screws were in the little bag inside the sleeve. She said the crease did not look serious but asked me to keep the packaging until she had tried one hinge on the pantry door. I left the sleeve upright beside the cupboard and put the signed delivery slip on the blue bowl with my keys. The tracking page later showed “delivered to Daniel Salcedo at 2:07 p.m.,” and its note said “signature captured.” The parcel was in our apartment, and the door still needed its old hinge until Mara had time to test the replacement.
